items.title: [Kernel] Coalesce reshape_and_cache stores by taking a KV block at a time
items.body:
## Overview

`reshape_and_cache` writes the paged KV cache one token per block, which makes every
store a column write and leaves the kernel at roughly 8% of achievable bandwidth. This
takes a whole KV block of tokens per block instead, so both destinations are contiguous.
**3.3x on the kernel; see the honest end-to-end read below before judging the value.**

This op has one caller in tree — `PagedAttention.write_to_paged_cache`, used only by
`vllm/v1/attention/backends/rocm_attn.py` — so the change is ROCm-only in practice.

## Claims

- **3.32x on the kernel in situ**, measured by profiler inside a real decode run
  (31264us -> 9405us over 128 calls), matching the microbenchmark.
- 1.56x to 3.80x in microbenchmark at 1024-8192 tokens, across aligned *and* misaligned
  slot mappings; no regression where the new path is not taken (1.00x).
- **Mean TTFT improves up to 1.17x under load** (1024-token prompts, concurrency 64;
  median 1.20x, p99 1.10x), which is where a faster KV write should show.
- **End-to-end throughput is unchanged** — the kernel is ~3% of prefill device time, so
  the ceiling is ~2.2% and measurement is flat. TPOT is likewise ~1.000x: this patch
  touches the prefill KV write, not the decode inner loop.
- Output is bit-identical to the unpatched kernel on every tested shape and slot layout;
  NIAH accuracy unchanged.
- No API change, no new kernel entry point, one file touched.

## Validation

**In-tree test:** `pytest tests/kernels/attention/test_cache.py -k "test_reshape_and_cache and not flash"` — 72 passed.

**Bitwise.** 380 cases — 5 `(heads, head_size, block_size)` combinations, bf16 and fp16,
1 to 8192 tokens, contiguous / mid-block / random / partly-masked slot mappings — hash
identically to the unpatched build (SHA-256 of raw cache bytes, not a tolerance).

**Kernel**, MI355X, bf16, head_size 128, block_size 16, HIP-graph replay, minimum of 15
replays of a 50-call graph. Slot mappings are built the way vLLM builds them: every
request draws its own shuffled blocks and requests are concatenated along the token
dimension, so a request whose length is not a multiple of `block_size` misaligns every
group after it.

| 8 heads, 8192 tokens | before | after | |
|---|---|---|---|
| one request, aligned | 105.56us | 31.14us | 3.39x |
| two requests [100, 8092] | 105.03us | 28.90us | 3.63x |
| eight requests, random lengths | 104.54us | 29.28us | 3.57x |
| one request, starts mid-block | 105.91us | 29.59us | 3.58x |
| one request, 10% slots masked | 103.32us | 27.22us | 3.80x |

At 1 head / 2048 tokens the launch is below the threshold, the per-token kernel runs
unchanged, and all five scenarios measure 1.00x.

**In situ**, Llama-3.1-8B, prefill of 8192 tokens x 8 sequences, prefix caching disabled:

| | device time | calls | share of step |
|---|---|---|---|
| `reshape_and_cache` (base) | 31264us | 128 | 3.15% |
| `reshape_and_cache_grouped` (patched) | 9405us | 128 | 0.98% |

The grouped path took all 128 calls with no fallback, and the 3.32x matches the
microbenchmark.

**End-to-end**, `VLLM_PLUGINS=` (upstream vLLM), default compiled path, ROCM_ATTN
backend, output throughput, mean of 4 reps with arms rotated across GPUs and benchmark
positions (measured GPU-to-GPU bias on identical builds: 0.21%):

- Llama-3.1-8B, 8 workloads from in=128/conc=1 to in=32768/conc=4: 0.995x to 1.008x
- Qwen3-30B-A3B, 6 workloads: 0.997x to 1.008x

Flat, as the 3.15% share predicts. The `in=200, conc=64` point deliberately exercises
misaligned, fallback-heavy slot runs: 1.008x, no regression.

**TTFT and TPOT.** Throughput is the wrong lens for a prefill-side KV write, so taking the
latency metrics directly — Llama-3.1-8B, in=1024:

| | base | patched | |
|---|---|---|---|
| mean TTFT, conc=32 | — | — | **1.064x** |
| mean TTFT, conc=64 | — | — | **1.170x** |
| median TTFT, conc=64 | — | — | **1.204x** |
| p99 TTFT, conc=64 | — | — | 1.101x |
| TPOT, all points | — | — | ~1.000x |

TTFT improves with load, which is the expected shape: more concurrent prefills mean more
KV-write work per step. Total benchmark duration is unchanged, so this is latency
redistribution rather than extra throughput — useful if TTFT under load is the SLO, not
if the goal is tokens per second.

**Models exercised, including those that showed nothing.** Reach was verified by loading
each model and reading vLLM's `Op '<x>' not present in model` log plus worker profiler
kernel counts:

| model | reaches `reshape_and_cache` | result |
|---|---|---|
| Llama-3.1-8B | yes (10080 calls) | throughput flat, TTFT as above |
| Qwen3-30B-A3B | yes (15120 calls) | throughput flat |
| DeepSeek-V4-Flash | no — fuses into `fused_qnorm_rope_kv_insert` | not benchmarked |
| MiniMax-M3 | no — aiter's KV writer | not benchmarked |
| Kimi-K3 | no — MLA uses `concat_and_cache_mla` | not benchmarked |
| Qwen3.8-27B | no — hybrid KV takes a Triton writer | not benchmarked |

**Accuracy.** lm_eval RULER NIAH (`niah_single_2`, `niah_multikey_1`) at 8192 and 32768
tokens, 100 docs per cell, both models: 1.0 in all cells, patched identical to base.

## Details

**Root cause.** The key cache is `[num_blocks, num_heads, head_size/x, block_size, x]` and
the value cache `[num_blocks, num_heads, head_size, block_size]`. With one token per
block, a thread writing the value cache touches elements `block_size` apart, so a cache
line is spent to move 2 bytes. At 4096 tokens the kernel moved 34 MB in 47us.

**Change.** Both layouts are contiguous in the other direction — key over
`(block_offset, i)`, value over `block_offset` — so a block now takes one KV block's worth
of tokens and stages `[block_size, head_size]` tiles through LDS, writing each destination
in its own order. Loads and stores are both contiguous, 16 bytes per thread. Two details
that mattered more than expected, each measured: the key and value halves load before a
*single* barrier (one barrier each serialises two independent streams and costs ~20%), and
the tile rows are padded so reading a tile down a column does not put every thread on one
LDS bank.

**Fallback.** A group only takes the fast path when its slots are one full, block-aligned
run. Ragged request boundaries, prefix-cache hits starting mid-block and masked tokens
(`slot < 0`) take the per-token path, which spreads `block_size * head_size/x` copies over
the whole block so it keeps the occupancy of the original kernel.

**Reach.** Over 64 checkpoints, at most 11 can route here: MLA (36) and hybrid-attention
(11) architectures cannot reach `reshape_and_cache` at all, and some GQA models bypass it
via an aiter fused KV writer.

**What this is worth.** A 3.3x kernel improvement that does not survive to end-to-end
throughput, because the kernel is ~3% of prefill device time. If the goal is throughput,
this is a null result at the step level. The case for it is that the kernel win is real
and verified in situ, the change is contained to one file with no API change, accuracy is
unchanged, and TTFT under load improves — plus it leaves less on the table as KV writes
grow with longer prefills. I would rather state that plainly than present the 3.3x alone.

**Limitation.** The fast path fires only when `block_size` consecutive tokens land on one
aligned KV block, which is not guaranteed in a multi-request batch. The misaligned path is
faster than base rather than slower, so the patch wins either way, but grouping by each
request's own aligned interval (via `query_start_loc`) would make the fast path fire far
more often. Not done here — happy to fold it in if preferred.

items.title: [Bugfix] Fix out-of-bounds block-table read in Triton unified attention
items.body:
## Overview

Fixes #61803. Sometimes the KV tile is wider than the KV block, for example the 32-wide prefill tile with block size 16. Then `kernel_unified_attention` reads block-table entries past the end of the sequence's row. compute-sanitizer reports invalid global reads at the unmasked block-table `tl.load`, and the launch fails. This PR masks that load with `tile_mask`, which every other load in the loop already uses. It makes the same change in the INT4 per-token-head kernel `_attn_packed`, which has a copy of the loop behind the same `unified_attention` entry point.

Compared with #61810, #61028 and #56862, this fix:

- Also masks the same load in `_attn_packed`, which `unified_attention` runs for `KVQuantMode.INT4_PER_TOKEN_HEAD`. With any of them, the INT4 form of the reproducer still gives 32 invalid reads at `int4_per_token_head.py:498` and a crash.
- Adds tests that fail on the old kernels. None of them adds a test, and the existing cases #61810 points to pass on the old code unless run under compute-sanitizer.

Compared with #56862, this fix:

- Does not pass the block-table width as a `tl.constexpr`. With #56862, Triton compiles a new kernel for each width: 5 variants of about 300 ms each for widths 3, 4, 5, 8 and 64, against 2 here. In the engine the width is fixed per KV-cache group, so this mostly costs direct callers and tests.

## Claims

- The reproducer from the issue now runs clean under compute-sanitizer. Before, it gave 32 invalid reads and a launch failure.
- The INT4 per-token-head path had the same out-of-bounds read, and it is fixed too.
- Output does not change: old and new kernels give bitwise-equal results in 14 modes.
- Two new regression tests, one per kernel, fail on the old kernels in plain pytest and pass with the fix.

## Validation

Setup: 1 x NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5090. vLLM at commit `df3bd094aeea829f27baa0a5282830464f601d9f` (`0.32.1rc1.dev117+gdf3bd094a`), with and without this patch. `compute-sanitizer` from CUDA 13.0. The bug was first reproduced in the `vllm/vllm-openai:nightly-df3bd094aeea829f27baa0a5282830464f601d9f` image (torch 2.14.0+cu130, triton 3.8.0), with the same result.

Reproducer: the script from the issue, plus the last `print`.

```python
import torch
from vllm.v1.attention.ops.triton_unified_attention import unified_attention

torch.manual_seed(0)
dev = "cuda"
D, Hq, Hkv, bs, NB = 64, 2, 2, 16, 4
ctx, qlen = 32, 2
nk = ctx + qlen
W = -(-nk // bs)
q = torch.randn(qlen, Hq, D, device=dev, dtype=torch.float16)
kc = torch.randn(NB, bs, Hkv, D, device=dev, dtype=torch.float16)
vc = torch.randn(NB, bs, Hkv, D, device=dev, dtype=torch.float16)
block_table = torch.randperm(NB, dtype=torch.int32, device=dev)[:W].reshape(1, W).clone()   # 12-byte allocation
out = torch.empty_like(q)
unified_attention(q=q, k=kc, v=vc, out=out,
                  cu_seqlens_q=torch.tensor([0, qlen], dtype=torch.int32, device=dev), max_seqlen_q=qlen,
                  seqused_k=torch.tensor([nk], dtype=torch.int32, device=dev), max_seqlen_k=nk,
                  softmax_scale=D ** -0.5, causal=True, window_size=(-1, -1), block_table=block_table,
                  softcap=0.0, q_descale=None, k_descale=None, v_descale=None)
torch.cuda.synchronize()
print("DONE no exception")
```

```
PYTORCH_NO_CUDA_MEMORY_CACHING=1 compute-sanitizer --tool memcheck python3 -P repro.py
```

Before the fix, 3 of 3 runs gave the same output: 32 invalid reads, then the launch failure.

```
========= Invalid __global__ read of size 4 bytes
=========     at kernel_unified_attention+0xdb0 in triton_unified_attention.py:431
=========     by thread (16,0,0) in block (0,0,0)
=========     Access to 0xd2cc6a0840c is out of bounds
=========     and is 1 bytes after the nearest allocation at 0xd2cc6a08400 of size 12 bytes
...
torch.AcceleratorError: CUDA error: unspecified launch failure
...
========= ERROR SUMMARY: 34 errors
```

After the fix, 3 of 3 runs were clean. A separate check session then ran it 3 more times, and all 3 were clean:

```
DONE no exception
========= ERROR SUMMARY: 0 errors
```

In the check session, I also loaded only the old `triton_unified_attention.py`. The 32 invalid reads at line 431 and `ERROR SUMMARY: 34 errors` came back, so the clean result comes from the patch.

I also ran the same script with an INT4 per-token-head cache. Before the fix, it gave 32 invalid reads at `int4_per_token_head.py:498` and `ERROR SUMMARY: 34 errors`. After the fix, it gave `ERROR SUMMARY: 0 errors` (1 run).

Tests: I ran them with `--noconftest`, because the local venv has no `tblib`. The new tests need nothing from `tests/conftest.py`.

- `pytest tests/kernels/attention/test_triton_unified_attention.py -k tile_wider_than_block_stays_within_block_table_row`: `2 passed`. With the old `triton_unified_attention.py`, the core test fails with `CUDA error: an illegal memory access was encountered`. With the old `int4_per_token_head.py`, the INT4 test fails the same way.
- `pytest tests/kernels/attention/test_triton_unified_attention.py -k 'not use_td'`: `1629 passed, 290 deselected`. The 290 `use_td` tests fail to compile on this GPU (`RuntimeError: PassManager::run failed`). The same tests fail with the old kernel.
- `pytest tests/quantization/test_per_token_kv_cache.py -k int4`: `3 failed, 23 passed`. The 3 failures are `test_reshape_and_cache_per_token_head[int4-...]` (`Tensor-likes are not close!`). They test the cache-write kernel, and they fail the same way with the old INT4 kernel.
- I compared old and new output in 14 modes: causal and non-causal prefill, sliding window, softcap, 2D and 3D decode, INT8 and INT4 per-token-head, and 48 sequences of length 4000. The block tables were like the engine's, with spare columns, so the old kernel does not fault. All outputs were bitwise equal. Kernel times moved by a few percent in both directions, which is noise at this size.
- `pre-commit` passes on the three changed files.

## Details

Root cause: `kernel_unified_attention` walks the KV sequence in tiles of `TILE_SIZE`. For every lane it loads `block_table[seq_offset // BLOCK_SIZE]`, with no mask. In the last tile, lanes at or past `max_seq_prefix_len` still compute a block index. When `TILE_SIZE > BLOCK_SIZE`, that index can be past the last block the sequence owns. In the reproducer, block size is 16 and `seq_len = 34`, so the row has 3 entries. `max_seqlen_q = 2` takes the 2D path with tile 32. Tile 1 covers positions 32 to 63, and lanes 16 to 31 (positions 48 to 63) load block 3. That is 12 bytes into a 12-byte table. The K/V loads and per-token-head scale loads that use this value are all masked with `tile_mask`, so the output was right. Only the read itself was out of bounds. Under compute-sanitizer this is an invalid read. If the table ends at unmapped memory, it is an illegal memory access.

The fix adds `mask=tile_mask, other=0` to that load. `compute_tile_loop_bounds` keeps `max_seq_prefix_len <= seq_len` in every mode, so a lane in the mask only reads a column the sequence owns. Every use of `physical_block_idx` is masked with the same `tile_mask`, so the `0` filler is never used. The `USE_TD` scalar load needs no change: it reads the block of `j * TILE_SIZE`, which is below `max_seq_prefix_len` for every `j < loop_hi`. The block table is not too narrow. The kernel's own tests and the engine both pass rows that are exactly as wide as the sequence needs, so padding in the caller would not fix the kernel. `_attn_packed` in `int4_per_token_head.py` is a line-for-line copy of this loop, with the same `compute_tile_loop_bounds` and `tile_mask`. It gets the same change.

Tests: a plain test cannot see this bug, because the bad value is never used and the read usually lands in mapped memory. The new tests use the CUDA VMM driver API (`cuda-bindings`, already pinned in `requirements/test/cuda.txt`). They place the block table at the very end of a mapped granule, with an unmapped one after it, so any read past the row faults. They use the reproducer's shape. The core test checks the output against `ref_paged_attn`. The INT4 test checks it against the same call with a normal block table. Both skip on non-CUDA platforms and when `cuda.bindings` is missing.

Not in this PR: the same unmasked block-table load is also in kernels behind other entry points: `triton_unified_attention_diffkv.py`, `turboquant_soa/triton_turboquant_unified_attention.py` and `ultraquant/triton_unified_attention.py`. The DiffKV one was seen to still read out of bounds. These can go in a follow-up, or in this PR if reviewers prefer.

items.title: [Perf] Enable efficient SDPA for Granite Speech block attention
items.body:
## Purpose

Granite Speech block attention currently passes five-dimensional Q, K, and V
tensors to scaled-dot-product attention and explicitly selects the math
backend. PyTorch's fused SDPA backends require four-dimensional inputs, so this
prevents the memory-efficient backend from being used.

This PR flattens the independent batch and block dimensions immediately before
SDPA, requests `EFFICIENT_ATTENTION` with `MATH` as a fallback, and restores the
original dimensions afterward.

The flatten and unflatten operations remain views for the production tensor
layout. Model interfaces, weights, Shaw relative-position scores, padding masks,
and attention scaling are unchanged.

## Test Plan

### Regression tests

```bash
python -m pytest -q \
  tests/models/multimodal/test_granite_speech_attention.py \
  tests/utils_/test_tensor_schema.py
```

The focused tests instantiate the real `GraniteSpeechConformerAttention`
module and compare its final output against the previous forced-math
implementation. They cover complete and partially padded final blocks, as well
as the requested backend order.

### Granite Speech 3.3 2B generation comparison

```bash
python -m pytest -q \
  'tests/models/multimodal/generation/test_granite_speech.py::test_models[10-128-2048-bfloat16-ibm-granite/granite-speech-3.3-2b-ibm-granite/granite-speech-3.3-2b]'
```

This test loads the 5.61 GiB `ibm-granite/granite-speech-3.3-2b` checkpoint
and its audio LoRA, runs one audio prompt through both vLLM and the Transformers
reference implementation in BF16, and compares generated tokens and top-10
log probabilities. It passed on the same RTX 4090.

### Lint

```bash
ruff check \
  tests/models/multimodal/test_granite_speech_attention.py \
  vllm/model_executor/models/granite_speech.py

ruff format --check \
  tests/models/multimodal/test_granite_speech_attention.py \
  vllm/model_executor/models/granite_speech.py
```

### RTX 4090 SDPA benchmark

Hardware/software: NVIDIA RTX 4090 (SM89, 24 GB), driver 580.76.05,
CUDA 13.2, PyTorch 2.13.0+cu132. No configuration changes.

The benchmark uses Granite Speech's production attention dimensions:

```text
context size = 200
heads        = 8
head dim     = 128
```

It covers FP16/BF16, batches 1 and 2, 1/2/4/8 blocks, and final-block
remainders 0/1/100/199. Each shape uses 50 warmups, 200 timed iterations,
and ten repeats.

| Metric | Result |
|---|---:|
| Geometric-mean SDPA speedup across 64 shapes | 4.82x |
| Minimum observed speedup | 3.96x |
| Maximum observed speedup | 6.99x |
| Math maximum peak allocation | 152,453,120 bytes |
| Efficient maximum peak allocation | 46,694,400 bytes |

All 64 numerical cases passed. The maximum absolute errors were
`0.0009765625` for FP16 and `0.0078125` for BF16.

The exact production attention module was also measured with BF16
`hidden_states=[1, 800, 1024]`, including LayerNorm, projections, Shaw
relative-position scores, attention, and the output projection:

| Variant | Median latency |
|---|---:|
| Original forced-math implementation | 528.48 us |
| Efficient-SDPA candidate | 306.15 us |
| Whole-module speedup | 1.73x |

The production-module maximum absolute error was `0.0009765625`.
Profiler output confirmed that the candidate executed
`aten::_scaled_dot_product_efficient_attention`; no layout-copy CUDA kernel
was introduced. CUDA Graph replay and `torch.compile(fullgraph=True)` smoke
tests also passed.

## Test Result

```text
23 passed (focused regression tests)
1 passed (Granite Speech 3.3 2B generation comparison)
```

Focused Ruff lint and format checks and `git diff --check` passed locally.

## Limitations

Performance results were collected on one RTX 4090. The end-to-end test
validates generation correctness against Transformers, but it is not an
end-to-end transcription throughput benchmark. The math backend remains
available as a fallback for devices where memory-efficient SDPA is unsupported.
Full upstream cross-backend CI still requires maintainer activation.

## Local follow-up validation (October 21)

Marked the pure PyTorch attention tests with the existing `skip_global_cleanup` marker. They create no engine or distributed state; unnecessary global cleanup segfaulted in PyTorch's macOS `empty_host_cache` after the test assertion passed. The attention implementation and assertions are unchanged.

Agent-run on macOS 15.1 ARM64, Python 3.12.13 and PyTorch 2.14.0:

```bash
PYTEST_DISABLE_PLUGIN_AUTOLOAD=1 .venv/bin/python -m pytest -q tests/models/multimodal/test_granite_speech_attention.py
# 3 passed
```

All applicable pre-commit hooks passed on both PR files, including Ruff and mypy; `git diff --check` also passed. This follow-up uses the PR source with local Python dependencies and no built vLLM native extensions. GPU tests, full-model evaluation and benchmarks were not rerun; earlier GPU evidence remains historical. These results are agent-run, not human-run.

## AI assistance

AI assistance was used during implementation, testing, benchmarking, and PR
drafting. The human contributor reviewed and takes responsibility for the
change and evidence.

items.title: [Attention] Allow num_splits > 1 on FA2 for speculative decode
items.body:
> **DRAFT — blocked on [vllm-project/flash-attention#176](https://github.com/vllm-project/flash-attention/pull/176).**
> Do not merge until that lands **and** `GIT_TAG` in `cmake/external_projects/vllm_flash_attn.cmake` is bumped past it. Merging earlier replaces a clean `NotImplementedError` with a `RuntimeError` raised from the unpatched `.so` — strictly worse for users.

## What this removes

```python
if num_splits > 1:
    raise NotImplementedError("FA2 does not support num_splits > 1")
```

Two lines, `vllm/vllm_flash_attn/flash_attn_interface.py`.

## Why it exists, and why it can go

It mirrors the C++ `TORCH_CHECK(num_splits <= 1, "not supported for varlen paged KV")`. That check is real: the FA2 combine kernel addressed O and LSE through `o_batch_stride`, which is **0** in a true varlen call, so it folded every sequence onto sequence 0. Correct at batch 1, silently wrong above it.

flash-attention#176 addresses O and LSE through `cu_seqlens_q` and skips rows past `actual_seqlen_q`, so the restriction no longer holds.

## Why this matters

`set_params_splitkv` is gated on `seqlenq_ngroups_swapped`, which requires `max_seqlen_q == 1`. Speculative decoding makes the verify pass carry `q_len = K+1`, so **split-K is silently disabled for every spec-decode step** — MTP, EAGLE, Medusa, draft-model and n-gram alike. The decode-attention grid collapses from 172 to 12 blocks: 12 of 128 SMs get work, ~3.5% of DRAM peak.

Measured end to end on RTX 4090 sm_89, Qwen3.6-27B-AWQ-INT4, TP2, MTP K=5, batch 1, ISL 16384, bf16 KV, clocks locked:

| arm | tok/s | TPOT ms | accept_len | step ms |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| base (x3) | 70.0 | 14.28 | 3.11 | 44.42 |
| patched (x2) | **108.9** | **9.19** | **3.20** | **29.41** |

**+55.4% tok/s, −35.6% TPOT**, noise ±0.07%, TTFT flat. Acceptance length rises slightly because split-K lands closer to an fp64 oracle. Full correctness matrix (96 cases incl. batch > 1 and non-uniform query lengths, red-before-green against unpatched vs patched `.so`) is in flash-attention#176.

## Not a duplicate

No open PR in this repo touches this guard; searched for `num_splits`/spec-decode/flash-attention combinations.

## AI assistance

**AI assistance (Claude) was used for this change.** The change and all measurements above were produced with AI assistance and reviewed by the human submitter.

items.title: TRITON_ATTN support for KV cache dtype fp8 on SM75 to pre-SM89
items.body:
# TRITON_ATTN support for KV cache dtype fp8 on SM75 to pre-SM89

Based on reviewer feedback on #45829 about the unprecedented quantity of inline assembly code for Triton, the conversion has been moved into dedicated CUDA conversion functions linked into Triton as LLVM bitcode, avoiding massive inline assembly in Triton.

## Purpose

Enable `--kv-cache-dtype fp8` on Turing (SM75) and Ampere (SM80/86) with `--attention-backend TRITON_ATTN`.

SM75–SM88 do not have the native `fp8e4nv` conversion available on SM89+. This change provides software conversion between FP8 E4M3 KV-cache storage and the activation dtype:

- FP8 E4M3 to and from FP16 on SM75
- FP8 E4M3 to and from BF16 on SM80–SM88
- Native conversion remains in use on SM89+

FP8 is only the KV-cache storage format. Each loaded KV tile is decoded to BF16 on SM80–SM88 or FP16 on SM75 before it is used by the attention dot product.

Encode performs saturating round-to-nearest-even conversion and is bit-exact with `torch.float8_e4m3fn`.

Decode reconstructs four BF16 or FP16 values from four packed FP8 bytes using SM75-compatible integer and `prmt` instructions. It is exact over all 256 FP8 byte values, including subnormals.

## Implementation

The conversion is exposed through two Triton entry points:

- `convert_to_fp8e4m3(x)` encodes FP16 or BF16 values for KV-cache storage.
- `convert_from_fp8e4m3(x, dtype)` decodes stored FP8 bytes to the requested activation dtype.

The dtype branches are resolved at Triton compile time.

The implementation consists of:

- `vllm/v1/attention/ops/fp8e4nv.py`: Triton entry points and LLVM extern bindings.
- `vllm/v1/attention/ops/fp8e4nv_helper.cu`: the CUDA conversion functions.
- `vllm/v1/attention/ops/fp8e4nv_helper_sm75.bc`: packaged LLVM bitcode generated from the CUDA source.
- `triton_reshape_and_cache_flash.py`: encodes scaled FP16 or BF16 values before storing them in the UINT8 KV cache.
- `triton_unified_attention.py`: decodes FP8-stored KV tiles to FP16 or BF16 and applies the per-tensor scale.

The software-conversion launches supply the bitcode through Triton’s `extern_libs` mechanism. Other launches are unchanged.

LLVM fully inlines the CUDA conversion functions. Final PTX and SASS contain no helper symbols, calls, or return boundaries.

The bitcode can be regenerated with the Clang command documented at the top of `fp8e4nv_helper.cu`.

## Test Plan

The serving matrix covers:

- Activation dtype: FP16 and BF16
- KV-cache dtype: FP16, BF16, and FP8
- Architectures: SM75, SM80, SM90, and SM100
- Attention backend explicitly set to `TRITON_ATTN`

Each KV-cache dtype is requested explicitly and confirmed from the engine configuration. `--kv-cache-dtype auto` is not used as the 16-bit comparison because it resolves to FP8 for the tested NVFP4 models.

Example throughput commands:

```bash
python benchmarks/benchmark_throughput.py \
  --model nvidia/Gemma-4-26B-A4B-NVFP4 \
  --attention-backend TRITON_ATTN \
  --kv-cache-dtype bfloat16 \
  --input-len 8192 \
  --output-len 8192 \
  --num-prompts 10

python benchmarks/benchmark_throughput.py \
  --model nvidia/Gemma-4-26B-A4B-NVFP4 \
  --attention-backend TRITON_ATTN \
  --kv-cache-dtype fp8 \
  --input-len 8192 \
  --output-len 8192 \
  --num-prompts 10
```

## Correctness

Focused conversion suite:

```bash
.venv/bin/python -B -m pytest \
  tests/kernels/attention/test_fp8e4nv_conversion.py -q
```

```text
8 passed
```

Conversion validation covers:

- All 65,536 FP16 input bit patterns
- All 65,536 BF16 input bit patterns
- All 256 FP8 byte values
- Saturating infinity and NaN encoding
- Exact subnormal decoding

Production integration validation covers:

- Reshape-and-cache FP8 writes
- Two-dimensional unified attention
- Segmented three-dimensional unified attention with 16 softmax partitions
- FP16 and BF16 encode tiles of 32, 64, 128, 256, and 512 elements
- Twenty representative decode layouts and warp configurations

All conversion comparisons are bit-exact.

Attention using an FP8-stored KV cache, software-decoded to BF16, was also compared with a Torch reference on A100:

- FP8-stored KV maximum absolute error: `0.0071`
- Native BF16 KV maximum absolute error: `0.0010`

Ruff check, Ruff format-check, and `git diff --check` pass.

## Inlining validation

The CUDA conversion functions are force-inlined into the generated Triton kernels.

For FP16 and BF16 encode at tile sizes 32, 64, 128, 256, and 512, the final kernels use:

- 168 instructions
- 24 registers per thread
- Zero calls
- Zero stack memory
- Zero shared memory
- Zero local memory

Decode retains the expected instruction and register counts across the tested production layouts and emits no calls.

Two FP16 decode orientations produce different ptxas scheduling and register allocation while retaining:

- 128 instructions
- 26 registers
- Zero calls
- Bit-exact output

Nsight Compute on the encode kernel reported:

- 100% theoretical occupancy
- 89.02% achieved occupancy
- 97.38% compute throughput
- 26.88% DRAM throughput
- 24 registers per thread
- Zero shared memory

Nsight Systems profiling completed successfully.

## Conversion throughput

Standalone pack-4 encode throughput in GB/s, single stream / four streams:

| Architecture and activation dtype | Throughput |
|---|---:|
| A100 FP16 | 465 / 643 |
| A100 BF16 | 466 / 644 |
| T4 FP16 | 191 / 213 |

Standalone decode throughput on A100 is approximately 930–957 GB/s.

## Attention-kernel performance

The attention computation remains in the activation dtype. The FP8-stored KV path includes the cost of decoding each loaded tile before the dot product.

Test configuration: 64 sequences, KV length 2048, GQA 8/2, and head size 128.

| Kernel | A100 | T4 |
|---|---:|---:|
| Unified attention reading native 16-bit KV | 301.8 µs | 4069 µs |
| Unified attention reading FP8-stored KV and decoding it to the activation dtype | 483.9 µs | 3812 µs |
| Reshape-and-cache writing native 16-bit KV | 118.2 µs | 582 µs |
| Reshape-and-cache encoding and writing FP8-stored KV | 132.7 µs | 581 µs |

The T4 figures represent one tested kernel configuration and are not generalized to other T4 workloads.

## End-to-end throughput

Single-request output tokens per second using the sequential schedule, ten prompts, NVFP4 weights, and explicitly requested KV-cache dtypes:

| Model | A100 16-bit KV → FP8-stored KV | H100 16-bit KV → FP8-stored KV | B200 16-bit KV → FP8-stored KV | T4 16-bit KV → FP8-stored KV |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Nano 9B | 152.5 → 148.9 | — | — | ~24.4 → ~24.5 |
| Nano 30B | 218.4 → 211.4 | — | — | Does not fit |
| Super, TP2 | 93.4 → 91.2 | — | — | Does not fit |
| Gemma 26B MoE | 113.3 → 87.6 | 164.4 → 169.7 | 209.7 → 207.8 | Does not fit |
| Gemma 31B dense | 36.2 → 30.9 | 55.6 → 55.6 | 79.5 → 78.9 | Does not fit |
| DiffGemma 26B | 107.0 → 57.5 | 247.2 → 200.0 | 371.4 → 318.3 | Does not fit |

Run-to-run variation on this metric is approximately 1–2%. Differences in that range are treated as no measurable change.

The T4 Nano 9B result is within this measurement noise and does not establish a general T4 performance advantage.

## Accuracy

Wikitext-2 perplexity, 16-bit KV / FP8-stored KV:

- Nano 9B: `15.257 / 15.268`
- Nano 30B: `13.371 / 13.410`
- Super: `5.488 / 5.483`

FP8-stored KV remains within 0.3% of the 16-bit KV result.

## KV-cache tradeoff

FP8 storage uses one byte per KV element instead of two, providing approximately twice the KV-cache capacity.

On SM75–SM88, each FP8-stored KV tile incurs software conversion to FP16 or BF16 when loaded. The resulting performance depends on the architecture, model, and number of KV rereads.

On SM89+, each FP8-stored KV tile is converted using the native hardware conversion before attention computation.

## Layout constraint

The decode helper requires a Triton layout assigning a multiple of four elements to each thread.

All current production unified-attention layouts satisfy this requirement, and the tested production layout matrix covers both two-dimensional and segmented three-dimensional attention.

## AI assistance

AI assistance was used in preparing this PR:

- Claude Code assisted with conversion-algorithm development.
- OpenAI Codex assisted with the CUDA/LLVM integration, code-generation validation, profiling, and PR preparation.

items.title: TRITON_ATTN support for KV cache dtype fp8 on sm75 to pre-sm89
items.body:
# TRITON_ATTN support for KV cache dtype fp8 on sm75 to pre-sm89

## Purpose

Enable `--kv-cache-dtype fp8` on Turing (SM75) and Ampere (SM80/86) with `--attention-backend TRITON_ATTN`, without any change to triton-lang.

SM75–SM88 have no native `fp8e4nv` cast; Triton kernels that emit `.to(tl.float8e4nv)` fail at compile time with *"type fp8e4nv not supported in this architecture"*. This PR adds direct `fp8e4m3 ↔ {fp16, bf16}` conversion via `tl.inline_asm_elementwise` so the KV cache can be stored and loaded as fp8 on Turing/Ampere. The conversion targets the activation dtype: direct `fp8 ↔ fp16` on SM75+ (Turing has no bf16 hardware type) and direct `fp8 ↔ bf16` on SM80+. On SM89+ the native `fp8e4nv` cast is used and this path is bypassed.

The conversion is exposed through one unified pair of entry points, with a single shipped algorithm — round-to-nearest-even encode, exact prmt-LUT decode:

- `vllm/v1/attention/ops/fp8e4nv.py` (new): `convert_to_fp8e4m3(x)` (encode — dispatches on `x.dtype` and **asserts** a 16-bit input, never silently casting) and `convert_from_fp8e4m3(x, dtype)` (decode to the requested dtype). The dtype branch is resolved at Triton compile time.
- `vllm/v1/attention/ops/fp8e4nv_fp16.py`, `fp8e4nv_bf16.py`: the `pack=4` SM75-legal integer-PTX literals (`and/or/shl/shr/add/sub/min/max/setp/selp/prmt/cvt.u32.u16` — no native fp8 cvt, no bf16, no video-SIMD) backing the RNE encode and the exact decode for each dtype. fp16 serves SM75 (no bf16 hardware type); bf16 serves SM80–88.
- `triton_attn.py`: gates `_fp8_software_conv` (SM75–88, CUDA); warns rather than raises; keeps the query unquantized on the software path (a query→fp8e4nv cast would fuse into the RoPE inductor kernel and fail to compile pre-SM89).
- `triton_reshape_and_cache_flash.py`: store path casts the scaled tile to the activation dtype and encodes via `convert_to_fp8e4m3` into the uint8 cache.  (The scaled tile `key / k_scale` is fp32 — a 16-bit value over an fp32 scale promotes — so casting to the activation dtype first selects the correct per-arch encoder.)
- `triton_unified_attention.py`: `_cast_kv_tile` decodes fp8 to the activation dtype via `convert_from_fp8e4m3` and applies the per-tensor scale in that dtype.

## Test Plan

Serve sanity (activation ∈ {bf16, fp16} × KV ∈ {bfloat16, float16, fp8}), and end-to-end throughput + perplexity via the precision sweep, on **A100 (SM80), H100 (SM90), B200 (SM100), and T4 (SM75)**, `--attention-backend TRITON_ATTN`, NVFP4 weights, batched `ppl + 1024+1024 + 8192+8192` per job. **TRITON_ATTN is force-selected for every run** (`--attention-backend TRITON_ATTN`, not the auto-chosen backend): this PR's fp8 software conversion lives in the Triton attention kernels, so the experiment deliberately characterizes the impact of fp8 KV-cache compression on these workloads **specifically under Triton attention**. Each KV dtype is **requested explicitly** and the resolved `kv_cache_dtype` is confirmed from each run's engine-config log — `--kv-cache-dtype auto` is **not** used as the 16-bit baseline, because for these NVFP4 models `auto` resolves to `fp8` (so an `auto`-vs-`fp8` comparison is fp8-vs-fp8).

### 16-bit-native baseline (bfloat16 on SM80+, float16 on T4) vs fp8:
```
python benchmarks/benchmark_throughput.py \
  --model nvidia/Gemma-4-26B-A4B-NVFP4 --attention-backend TRITON_ATTN \
  --kv-cache-dtype bfloat16 --input-len 8192 --output-len 8192 --num-prompts 10   # baseline
python benchmarks/benchmark_throughput.py \
  --model nvidia/Gemma-4-26B-A4B-NVFP4 --attention-backend TRITON_ATTN \
  --kv-cache-dtype fp8 --input-len 8192 --output-len 8192 --num-prompts 10   # fp8
```

## Test Result

The unified conversion and the attention/store integration are validated on A100 (SM80) for both activation dtypes:

- **Conversion suite** (`tests/kernels/attention/test_fp8e4nv_conversion.py`): `4 passed` — decode exact over all 254 finite fp8 bytes and RNE encode bit-exact vs the saturating `torch.float8_e4m3fn` reference, for fp16 and
bf16; the SM89+ native cross-checks skip on SM80.
- **Flash-attention integration** (the merged `convert_to/from` inside the live `unified_attention` + `reshape_and_cache` kernels): the correctness gate passes — fp8-software attention vs a torch reference is `max_abs_err = 0.0071` (native bf16 `0.0010`); `unified_attention` native(bf16) 303 µs vs fp8-software 426 µs; `reshape_and_cache` store native 123 µs vs fp8 ~135 µs (round-mode-independent now that encode is RNE-only).

## Design Exploration and Design Tradeoff Analysis

The single shipped algorithm above was chosen after characterizing the alternatives — three encode rounding modes (`rn`/`rne`/`trunc`) and three decode implementations (arithmetic `region`, byte-LUT `lut`, low-register prmt-LUT `lut2`) — at three levels (standalone microbench, the flash-attention kernel, and full end-to-end). Those commits remain in this branch's history.

### Conversion correctness

`rne` is **bit-exact** vs `torch.float8_e4m3fn` over all finite inputs (all 254 finite fp8 bytes for decode; all 65,536 fp16/bf16 patterns for encode, ±inf/±NaN saturating); `rn` is within 1 fp8-code ULP and `trunc` within 2; decode is exact. On SM89+ the same checks run against the native fp8 cvt.

### Conversion throughput (standalone kernel, pack=4, GB/s, single-stream / 4-stream)

| | rn | rne | trunc |
|---|---|---|---|
| A100 (SM80) fp16 | 540 / 794 | 465 / 643 | 612 / 960 |
| A100 (SM80) bf16 | 541 / 795 | 466 / 644 | 569 / 858 |
| T4 (SM75) fp16 | 127 / 139 | 191 / 213 | 210 / 242 |

Standalone, all decode variants run ~930–957 GB/s on A100 with no meaningful spread (the bare kernel has spare registers). The low-register decode (`lut2`, 35 reg vs the naïve LUT's 46) only pays off **inside** the attention kernel, where register pressure exists.

### Flash-attention kernel — conversion integrated (decode-heavy: 64 seqs, kv_len 2048, GQA 8/2, head 128)

| kernel | A100 | T4 |
|---|---|---|
| `unified_attention`, native KV | 301.8 µs | 4069 µs |
| `unified_attention`, fp8 KV (`lut2` decode) | 483.9 µs (**1.60×**) | 3812 µs(**0.94×**) |
|  `reshape_and_cache`, native store | 118.2 µs | 582 µs |
| `reshape_and_cache`, fp8 store `rne`/`rn`/`trunc` | 132.7 / 132.8 / 131.2 µs | 581 / 574 / 580 µs |
| in-attention decode `lut2` vs `lut` | no difference (128-reg ceiling) | 4097 vs 4172 µs (~1.8%) |

The fp8 store is rounding-mode-neutral on both archs. The compute-rich A100 pays ~60% on the attention kernel for the software decode; the bandwidth-bound T4 *gains* (0.94×) because halving KV traffic outweighs the decode.

### End-to-end — fp8 KV vs 16-bit-float native (bfloat16 SM80+, float16 T4), TRITON_ATTN

Single-request **peak-latency** out_tok/s (`SEQUENTIAL` schedule, num-prompts=10), NVFP4 weights, TP1 (super TP2). Each dtype requested explicitly; resolved `kv_cache_dtype` confirmed per run. One run per cell.

| model | A100/SM80 16b → fp8 | H100/SM90 16b → fp8 | B200/SM100 16b → fp8 | T4/SM75 16b → fp8 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| nano9b (hybrid-Mamba, 4 attn layers) | 152.5 → 148.9 (−2%) | — | — | ~24.4 → ~24.5 (≈) |
| nano30 | 218.4 → 211.4 (−3%) | — | — | n/a (19 GB > 16) |
| super (TP2) | 93.4 → 91.2 (−2%) | — | — | n/a |
| gemma26b (MoE) | 113.3 → 87.6 (**−23%**) | 164.4 → 169.7 (≈) | 209.7 → 207.8 (≈) | n/a (18 GB > 16) |
| gemma31b (dense) | 36.2 → 30.9 (−15%) | 55.6 → 55.6 (≈) | 79.5 → 78.9 (≈) | n/a |
| diffgemma26b (block-diffusion) | 107.0 → 57.5 (**−46%**) | 247.2 → 200.0 (−19%) | 371.4 → 318.3 (−14%) | n/a |

**Reading the table.** Run-to-run noise on this metric is ~1–2% (one cell, gemma26b/H100, even shows fp8 *faster* than bf16 — unphysical, i.e. noise). So treat every **"≈"** and the **nano/super −2–3%** as *no measurable fp8 cost*; only the deltas ≳10% (A100 gemma/diffgemma; diffgemma on H100/B200) are confidently real. "—" = not run this sweep; "n/a" = does not fit 16 GB. nano/super were run on A100 only; gemma on A100/H100/B200; T4 fits only nano9b.

**Accuracy (perplexity, wikitext-2, 16b / fp8):** nano9b 15.257 / 15.268 · nano30 13.371 / 13.410 · super 5.488 / 5.483 — fp8 is within **≤0.3%** of 16-bit. The three encode rounding modes (`rne`/`rn`/`trunc`) are e2e-equivalent (±0.3% ppl, identical throughput) — `rne` (bit-exact) is the safe default. (The gemma wikitext-ppl path returns garbage for **both** bf16 and fp8 in this harness, so gemma ppl is omitted — a harness artifact, not an fp8 effect.)

### Analysis

There are two separate questions: **which conversion algorithm**, and **whether to convert at all**. The data answers them very differently.

#### (1) The conversion-algorithm choice: encode is e2e-free, the decode is not 

To decide the algorithm on evidence rather than microbench, all six `{rne, rn, trunc} × {lut2, region}` combinations were run **end-to-end** on the three attention-heavy NVFP4 models — the regime where the fp8-KV conversion is most expensive (gemma 15–46% on the cross-arch table above), so any per-algorithm difference is at its largest. A100 (SM80, the software-conversion path), `--attention-backend TRITON_ATTN`, `--kv-cache-dtype fp8`, NVFP4 weights, TP1, 8192+8192, single-request out_tok/s (one run/cell; the engine vLLM build SHA and the per-cell `encode rounding:` / `decode impl:` selection were confirmed from each run's log):

The two axes are independent. The three **encode** modes trade accuracy for integer-op count: `rne` (round-to-nearest-even) is bit-exact vs `torch.float8_e4m3fn` but spends extra ops resolving the even-tie case, `rn` (round-to-nearest, ties-away) is within 1 fp8-code ULP, and `trunc` (round-toward-zero) simply drops the residual mantissa bits for the lowest op count at ≤2 ULP. The two **decode** implementations differ in *how* they reconstruct the 16-bit value from an fp8 byte: `region` does it **arithmetically** — branching on the exponent into the normal / subnormal / overflow ranges and rebuilding the bits with shifts, adds, and predicated= `selp` selects — which is correct but ALU- and register-heavy; `lut2` instead treats the conversion as a **byte lookup**, using the SM75-legal `prmt` byte-permute as the lookup table for the result bytes (exact including subnormals) and folding the byte-isolate-and-shift into the `prmt` selector, so the whole decode costs **35 registers vs the naïve byte-LUT's 46**. Register pressure is the deciding axis: the decode runs *inside* the attention kernel, whose live Q/K/V tiles and softmax accumulators already crowd the register file, so the `region` decode's extra live values throttle occupancy on attention-heavy work — which is precisely why the lower-register `lut2` pulls ahead end-to-end below, even though the standalone microbench (spare registers, no pressure) showed the decodes as equal.

| model | `lut2` rne / rn / trunc | `region` rne / rn / trunc |
|---|---|---|
| gemma26b (MoE) | 86.5 / 88.3 / 86.6 | 82.9 / 82.9 / 84.0 |
| gemma31b (dense) | 30.8 / 30.5 / 30.6 | 29.6 / 29.6 / 29.7 |
| diffgemma26b (block-diffusion) | 59.6 / 59.6 / 61.2 | 53.2 / 53.9 / 53.2 |

**Encode rounding is e2e-free.** With the decode held fixed, `rne` / `rn` / `trunc` agree to ≤~1–2% on every model — run-to-run noise, with no systematic ordering (within-run variance flags the one apparent outlier, diffgemma
`trunc·lut2` +2.7%, as a high-variance cell, not a real gain). This is consistent with the rounding-mode-neutral store kernel (131–133 µs, <1% spread) and the ±0.3% ppl above. So encode rounding carries no e2e penalty — **ship `rne`** (bit-exact, no overhead relative to lower precision choices).

**The decode does *not* come free — `lut2` is materially faster than `region`.** Holding the encode fixed, the shipped low-register prmt-LUT decode (`lut2`) beats the region-arithmetic decode (`region`) end-to-end by **~4% on gemma dense/MoE and ~10% on diffgemma**. The standalone microbench hid this (all decodes ~930–957 GB/s with spare registers; even the in-kernel `lut2`-vs-`lut` comparison showed no A100 difference at the 128-register
ceiling) — but the relevant comparison is `lut2` vs the *arithmetic* `region` decode on attention-heavy models, and there the region decode's higher op/register cost lands on the critical path. diffgemma makes it largest: its
block-diffusion schedule re-reads the KV many times per token (see §(2)), so each extra decode instruction is paid repeatedly, widening the gap to ~10%. This is the measured justification for the shipped decode: **`lut2` is not merely "lower-register at no penalty" — it is 4–10% faster than the alternative exactly where attention dominates.**

So the algorithm choice is settled by data, not preference: **ship `rne`\ (free, bit-exact) + `lut2` (4–10% faster than `region` on attention-heavy decode).**

#### (2) The conversion *cost* (fp8-decode vs 16-bit no-decode) = per-read decode expense × read count

`_cast_kv_tile` widens fp8 KV back to the activation dtype on *every* KV-tile read (the dot runs in bf16/fp16, not fp8). The cost is that decode, paid once per read. Three regimes:

- **SM75–88 — this PR's software conversion path (the path under review).** Standalone the software decode adds ~60% to the attention kernel on A100 (`unified_attention` 301.8 → 483.9 µs); end-to-end that dilutes to a model-level cost **scaling with attention weight** — gemma dense/MoE 15–46%, while hybrid-Mamba nemotron-nano (4 attention layers → KV touches little compute) is **≤2–3% and not worth analyzing further**. On the bandwidth-bound **T4 the software decode is a net win** — fp8-KV attention is *faster* than fp16 (0.94×), since halving KV traffic outweighs the decode.

- **SM89+ (H100/B200) — native cvt; shown as a control, pre-existing and not this PR's path.** Here fp8 KV uses the hardware cvt, so these numbers reflect the conversion-*path* overhead with the **native cvt** — a single fp8↔bf16 cvt instruction per KV read: quasi-free, but still imposing that instruction's cost plus whatever schedule disruption it causes in the kernel. Its per-read cost is small enough to sit within run-to-run noise for autoregressive decode (gemma26b/gemma31b fp8 ≈ bf16), but it is real and accumulates: diffgemma's −14–19% below is literally that native-cvt cost paid over the block-denoising re-reads. This is the clean control proving the A100 cost is specifically the *software decode*: same model, same path, only the decode expense changes (diffgemma −46% A100 software vs −14–19% H100/B200 native cvt).

- **diffgemma — the diffusion outlier.** diffgemma generates by **block-diffusion denoising rather than autoregressive decode**: it re-attends over the block's KV at every denoising step, so each KV element is decoded\ *several times per output token* instead of once as in autoregressive generation. That is why it carries a conversion cost on **every** arch — including H100/B200, where the native cvt's per-read *overhead* on the autoregressive gemmas is within noise (fp8 ≈ bf16): even that single-instruction cvt, multiplied by the block-denoising re-read count, accumulates to −14–19% (and to −46% under the A100 software decode). This is a property of the block-diffusion attention schedule, not of the conversion code; it is the one model where the KV-decode path stays on the critical path regardless of cvt cost.

#### Net

fp8 KV delivers its intended win — ~2× KV-cache capacity (1 byte/element vs 2) at ≈-or-better throughput — exactly where it should: bandwidth-bound **T4** (about same throughput -- marginally but repeatably faster), **SM89+** (the fp8 *conversion* is quasi-free → fp8 ≈ bf16 throughput), and low-attention models (**nano ≤2%**). The throughput cost is material only for attention-heavy autoregressive decode on the SM75–88 software path (**gemma on A100**, 15–46%) and for the block-diffusion pattern (**diffgemma**, all archs) — and even there it is often the right tradeoff for a KV cache: the alternative, serving the same 2× context with 16-bit KV, needs ~2× the KV memory and therefore more GPUs, which is almost always a higher expense and is not even possible in every environment. Trading some attention throughput for 2× KV capacity on the *same* hardware is frequently the cheaper option.

AI assistance (Claude Code) in the preparation of this PR.

items.title: fix: add TQFullAttentionSpec guard in v1 _reshape_kv_cache_tensors
items.body:
## Problem

vLLM v1 engine crashes with `ValueError: Unknown TurboQuant cache dtype: 'auto'` when using `--kv-cache-dtype turboquant_*` with hybrid Mamba+Attention models (e.g. Qwen3.5-MoE / Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-AWQ).

## Root Cause

`_reshape_kv_cache_tensors` in `v1/worker/gpu_model_runner.py:7397` sets `layer_cache_dtype_str = "auto"` for any layer with `kv_quant_mode == KVQuantMode.NONE`. This `"auto"` string is then passed to `TurboQuantConfig.from_cache_dtype()` which only accepts explicit presets (`turboquant_4bit_nc`, etc.).

The non-v1 path (`v1/worker/gpu/attn_utils.py:312-315`) already guards against this:

```python
layer_cache_dtype = (
    "auto"
    if kv_cache_spec.kv_quant_mode == KVQuantMode.NONE
    and not isinstance(kv_cache_spec, TQFullAttentionSpec)  # <-- this guard exists here
    else cache_dtype
)
```

The v1 engine path is missing the same guard.

## Fix

Add the same `TQFullAttentionSpec` guard to the v1 engine path:

1. Import `TQFullAttentionSpec` from `vllm.v1.kv_cache_interface`
2. Add `and not isinstance(kv_cache_spec, TQFullAttentionSpec)` to the condition in `gpu_model_runner.py`

This ensures TurboQuant layers always receive the correct cache dtype string, while genuinely unquantized layers (skipped via `--kv-cache-dtype-skip-layers`) still get `"auto"`.

## Reproduction

```bash
vllm serve QuantTrio/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-AWQ   --kv-cache-dtype turboquant_4bit_nc   --tensor-parallel-size 2   --enforce-eager
```

Without fix: `ValueError: Unknown TurboQuant cache dtype: 'auto'. Valid presets: turboquant_k8v4, turboquant_4bit_nc, ...`

With fix: server starts successfully.

## Tested

Verified on 2x RTX 3060 12GB with Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-AWQ (hybrid MoE, 35B/3B active, 256 experts, 8 active).

items.title: [Bug]: nvfp4 KV cache silently corrupt under token-major (BLNHC) KV-cache layout — writer/reader stride mismatch
items.body:
> **Disclosure:** this report was drafted with the assistance of an AI agent; the root-cause analysis, the repro, and the environment details below were verified by hand on the machine described in the Environment section.


## Environment

```
vLLM 0.30.0 (vllm/vllm-openai:v0.30.0)
Python 3.12.3, PyTorch 2.13.0+cu130 (CUDA 13.0)
GPU: NVIDIA RTX PRO 5000 Blackwell (SM120), 2x, TP2 + EP
Model: nvidia/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4 (Qwen4Exp/QSA sparse-attention path, modelopt-mixed)
Flags: --kv-cache-dtype nvfp4 --tensor-parallel-size 2 --enable-expert-parallel
Boot log: "Using BLNHC KV cache layout." (engine default)
```

## 🐛 Describe the bug

Running any model on the QSA path (Qwen3.8-Flash-Next) with `--kv-cache-dtype nvfp4`
on v0.30.0 produces **incoherent output at every context length** — short prompts
included. It is silent: no exception, no crash, no Xid, no AER; the server stays up
and returns plausible-looking token streams. Deterministic sanity checks that a
healthy model answers trivially (arithmetic, capital-of-Japan, spell-a-word-backwards)
all fail, and ~253k-token needle retrieval finds 0 of N needles.

### Root cause

The stock C++ nvfp4 KV-cache **write** kernel
(`csrc/libtorch_stable/nvfp4_kv_cache_kernels.cu`,
`reshape_and_cache_nvfp4_dispatch`) derives head/token **data** strides and the
data|scale region split from **internal head-major (HND) formulas** after
detecting HND vs NHD from `stride(2) > stride(1)`. The standard **reader** helper
(`vllm/utils/torch_utils.py: nvfp4_split_data_scale`) instead scales the
*actual* tensor strides by `data_dim/full_dim`.

The two agree only for a head-major physical page. The engine's layout resolver
(`vllm/v1/attention/backends/utils.py: resolve_kv_cache_layout`) picks the first
entry of the backend's `supported_kv_cache_layouts()`; for the QSA backend that is
**BLNHC** (token-major: per-token rows of `2H` head slots × `full_dim` bytes, K/V
slots interleaved per token, each slot packing data+scale). Under that layout the
writer's internal formulas place head `h`, token `t`, and the scale region at
offsets that do not match where the reader looks → every K/V write (and its block
scales) lands in the wrong bytes, and the reader faithfully reads the garbage back.

The asymmetry that makes this easy to miss: a writer run against a contiguous or
head-major buffer (e.g. any test that builds `torch.zeros(...)` and passes
`[B, H, N, C]`) is self-consistent and passes. The token-major page is only ever
produced by the real allocator, so the bug is invisible to round-trip tests that
don't recreate the engine's physical layout.

### What we ruled out (this is not those)

- **QSA read kernel** (PR #54846): numerically correct. Round-trips at production
  geometry — multi-block block_table, multi-split/K + merge, multi-request,
  4096-row prefill chunks, top-k 2048 — match a bf16 reference on the
  dequantized cache to ≤6e-5.
- **MTP / speculative decoding**: garbage reproduced with MTP fully off.
- **Per-layer quant scales**: the modelopt-mixed checkpoint carries no per-layer
  K/V/q scale tensors; stock `set_default_quant_scales` leaves `_k_scale`/`_v_scale`
  = 1.0, matching all passing round-trips.

The failure is in the **write path / cache layout** — exactly where a
writer/reader stride mismatch lives.

### Evidence (writer→reader round-trip at production geometry B=2, N=5568, H=2, D=256)

| physical layout | K relerr | V relerr | verdict |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| token-major (BLNHC — engine default) | **1.4644** | **1.2185** | corrupt |
| head-major (BLHNC) | **0.0895** | **0.0895** | correct (pure nvfp4 rounding) |

0.0895 is the expected nvfp4 (E2M1 + E4M3 block scale) quantization error —
the same value a known-good round-trip produces. 1.46 / 1.22 means the
dequantized cache is unrelated to the input.

### Minimal reproduction

Self-contained script (one GPU, ~300 MB VRAM at production geometry; `REPRO_B`/
`REPRO_N` env vars shrink it on a busy box — the mismatch is a layout property,
not a size property):

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Stock nvfp4 KV writer vs reader under the two physical per-layer layouts
vLLM may resolve. Token-major (BLNHC, engine default for QSA) -> corrupt."""
import os, torch
from vllm.v1.attention.backends.fa_utils import reshape_and_cache_flash
from vllm.utils.torch_utils import nvfp4_split_data_scale

DEV = "cuda"
B = int(os.environ.get("REPRO_B", 2))
H, D = 2, 256
N = int(os.environ.get("REPRO_N", 5568))
HD, FD = 2 * H, D // 2 + D // 16      # K+V slots; nvfp4 full_dim = 144
PAGE, SD = HD * N * FD, D // 16
_E2M1 = [0.0, 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0, 6.0]

def _e4m3(bits):
    p = bits.to(torch.int32) & 0x7F
    e, m = (p >> 3) & 0x0F, p & 0x7
    v = torch.where(e == 0, m.float() / 512.0,
                    torch.pow(2.0, e.float() - 7.0) * (1.0 + m.float() / 8.0))
    return torch.where(p == 0, torch.zeros_like(v), v)

def _scale_coords(n, swizzled, dev):
    t, s = torch.arange(n, device=dev).view(-1, 1), torch.arange(SD, device=dev).view(1, -1)
    if not swizzled:
        return t.expand(n, SD), s.expand(n, SD)
    g = SD // 4
    return (t // 4) * 4 + (s // g), (s % g) * 4 + (t % 4)

def dequant_side(side, swizzled, device):
    data, scales = nvfp4_split_data_scale(side)
    data, scales = data.contiguous(), scales.view(torch.uint8)
    b, n, h, _ = data.shape
    table = torch.tensor(_E2M1 + [-v for v in _E2M1], dtype=torch.float32, device=device)
    nib = torch.stack((data & 0x0F, (data >> 4) & 0x0F), dim=-1)
    vals = table[nib.reshape(b, n, h, D).long()]
    ti, si = _scale_coords(n, swizzled, device)
    picked = scales[:, ti.reshape(-1), :, :].reshape(b, n, SD, h, SD)
    sel = si.view(1, n, SD, 1, 1).expand(b, n, SD, h, 1)
    picked = torch.gather(picked, 4, sel).squeeze(4).permute(0, 1, 3, 2)
    return (vals * _e4m3(picked).repeat_interleave(16, dim=3)).to(torch.bfloat16)

def relerr(a, b):
    a, b = a.to(torch.float64), b.to(torch.float64)
    return ((a - b).abs().mean() / b.abs().mean().clamp(min=1e-12)).item()

def run(order):
    raw = torch.zeros(B * PAGE, dtype=torch.uint8, device=DEV)
    view = (torch.as_strided(raw, (B, HD, N, FD), (PAGE, FD, HD * FD, 1)) if order == "token-major"
            else torch.as_strided(raw, (B, HD, N, FD), (PAGE, N * FD, FD, 1)))
    g = torch.Generator(device=DEV); g.manual_seed(0)
    key = (torch.randn(B * N, H, D, device=DEV, generator=g) * 0.5).bfloat16()
    val = (torch.randn(B * N, H, D, device=DEV, generator=g) * 0.5).bfloat16()
    scale = torch.tensor(1.0, dtype=torch.float32, device=DEV)
    slots = torch.arange(B * N, dtype=torch.int64, device=DEV)
    reshape_and_cache_flash(key, val, view[:, :H].transpose(1, 2),
                            view[:, H:].transpose(1, 2), slots, "nvfp4", scale, scale)
    torch.cuda.synchronize()
    k_dq = dequant_side(view[:, :H].transpose(1, 2), False, DEV)
    v_dq = dequant_side(view[:, H:].transpose(1, 2), True, DEV)
    kr, vr = relerr(k_dq.reshape(B*N, H, D), key), relerr(v_dq.reshape(B*N, H, D), val)
    print(f"{order:13s}  K relerr={kr:.4f}  V relerr={vr:.4f}  "
          f"-> {'CORRUPT' if max(kr, vr) > 0.3 else 'OK (nvfp4 rounding)'}")

run("token-major")   # engine default for QSA (BLNHC)
run("head-major")    # VLLM_KV_CACHE_LAYOUT=BLHNC
```

Output (measured on the box above):

```
token-major    K relerr=1.4644  V relerr=1.2185  -> CORRUPT
head-major     K relerr=0.0895  V relerr=0.0895  -> OK (nvfp4 rounding)
```

### Workaround (confirmed on the full model)

Force the head-major layout the writer expects:

```
VLLM_KV_CACHE_LAYOUT=BLHNC
```

Same server becomes coherent: quality gate 7/7, ~253k-context needle retrieval
5/6, C=3 full-context concurrency clean. (BLHNC = block-compact, L/B outermost,
so it also satisfies the hybrid/KV-group layout constraints.)

### Suggested upstream fix (pick one)

1. **Make the writer layout-aware** (preferred): derive head/token data strides
   and the data|scale region offsets from the *actual* `key_cache` strides,
   mirroring what `nvfp4_split_data_scale` does on the read side — any layout works.
2. **Guard it**: if the resolved layout is token-major (NHD/BLNHC), reject
   `--kv-cache-dtype nvfp4` with a clear error, or write via a token-major path.
   A silent corrupt cache is the worst outcome.
3. **Document + reorder**: at minimum, document that nvfp4 KV requires a
   head-major layout, and consider having backends that list
   `(BLNHC, BLHNC)` prefer the head-major one when nvfp4 KV is in use.

### References

- Writer: `csrc/libtorch_stable/nvfp4_kv_cache_kernels.cu`
  (`reshape_and_cache_nvfp4_dispatch` / `reshape_and_cache_nvfp4_kernel`)
- Reader: `vllm/utils/torch_utils.py` (`nvfp4_split_data_scale`)
- QSA read kernel + model integration: PR #54846
- Layout resolver: `vllm/v1/attention/backends/utils.py` (`resolve_kv_cache_layout`);
  layouts: `vllm/v1/kv_cache_layout.py`
- Related nvfp4 KV work: #40177, #59342 — orthogonal to those; this is the
  shared stock **writer**, not a specific attention backend's read path.

### 🐛 Describe the bug

## Summary

Long-running vLLM engine processes leak host memory (VmRSS/VmData) on paths where a
libtorch stable-ABI custom op with a `str` argument is dispatched **eagerly** in the hot
loop. Each such call leaks ~48 bytes; over hours this grows unbounded and can OOM the
engine (~0.5 GB/hour under continuous load in our reproduction).

The root cause is **not in vLLM** — it is a bug in PyTorch's stable ABI, which
heap-allocates a `std::string` when unboxing a `str` argument and never frees it.

**Upstream issue:** https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/191340

## Where it hits vLLM

`reshape_and_cache_flash` is registered as a stable op with a `str kv_cache_dtype`
argument:

- schema: `csrc/libtorch_stable/torch_bindings.cpp`
  (`reshape_and_cache_flash(Tensor key, ... str kv_cache_dtype, ...) -> ()`)
- impl:   `csrc/libtorch_stable/cache_kernels.cu`
  (`void reshape_and_cache_flash(..., const std::string& kv_cache_dtype, ...)`)
- bind:   `ops.impl("reshape_and_cache_flash", TORCH_BOX(&reshape_and_cache_flash))`

On most paths this op is captured into a CUDA graph and replayed, so it is not
re-dispatched per step and the leak does not accumulate. But on the **Voxtral/Whisper
realtime streaming** path it is dispatched eagerly — once per attention layer per decode
step — so every KV-cache write leaks and the process grows without bound.

Any other eagerly-dispatched stable op with a `str` argument is affected the same way.

## Symptoms

- Steady, linear host-memory growth (VmRSS/VmData) proportional to decode steps, not to
  batch size or sequence length.
- Invisible to `tracemalloc` (the allocation is C++-side, not Python).
- Not reclaimed by `malloc_trim(0)` — the memory is live, not fragmentation.
- glibc `mallinfo2().uordblks` grows in lockstep with RSS.
- Present only on eager (non-CUDA-graph) dispatch paths.

## Root cause (upstream)

In PyTorch's `torch/csrc/stable/stableivalue_conversions.h`, the `str` → `std::string`
unboxing (`ToImpl<std::string>::call`) does:

```cpp
auto strptr = new std::string(data, length);   // heap-allocated
TORCH_ERROR_CODE_CHECK(torch_delete_string(handle));
return *strptr;                                 // returns a COPY; *strptr is never deleted
```

Each unbox orphans one heap-allocated `std::string` control object (~48 bytes:
`sizeof(std::string)` + allocator overhead; the value's characters are irrelevant since
short strings like `"auto"` fit small-string optimization). Fix is upstream: construct the
string on the stack instead of with `new`. See
https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/191340 for details and the patch.

## Impact on vLLM

- Realtime/streaming ASR paths (Voxtral, Whisper) that dispatch KV-cache writes eagerly
  leak continuously and can OOM long-running servers.
- Standard batched/CUDA-graph serving is largely unaffected because the op is replayed,
  not re-dispatched.

## Fix / mitigation

- **Real fix:** upstream PyTorch (https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/191340). The
  fix is header-only in the stable ABI, so vLLM's custom-op `.so` must be recompiled.
- **Possible vLLM-side mitigations** while waiting for an upstream release:
  - Avoid re-dispatching stable ops with `str` arguments in eager hot loops (e.g. pass the
    dtype as an enum/int rather than a `str`, if a non-`str` schema is feasible).
  - Ensure the affected streaming paths use CUDA-graph capture/replay where possible.

## Reproduction

Minimal, self-contained (CPU-only) reproduction of the underlying leak — two no-op stable
ops identical except one takes a `str` — is in the upstream issue:
https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/191340

## Environment

```
torch: 2.11.0+cu130
CUDA:  13.0
OS:    Linux (x86_64)
```

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

items.title: [Bugfix] Unify per-layer KV cache dtype selection across v1/v2 model runners
items.body:
Edit:
The main issues has been resolved in #47609 and #47716 . This PR now just make the two fix in sync for both v1 and v2 runner.

## Purpose

  1. DeepSeek V4 Flash on SM121: `Expected packed SM120 DSV4 swa_kv_cache head dim 584, got 512` (reported in #42890 comments)

  **Root cause:** #42890 passes `"auto"` to `get_kv_cache_shape()` when `spec.kv_quant_mode == NONE` (so skipped layers get the unquantized shape). But specs whose layout is encoded in the dtype **string** (`fp8_ds_mla`, `turboquant_*`) also have `kv_quant_mode == NONE`, so they wrongly received `"auto"`.

  **Fix:** trust `spec.cache_dtype_str` when present (already on the MLA specs from #40860), falling back to the skip-layer heuristic otherwise. Adds the field to
  `TQFullAttentionSpec` and sets it at construction. No behavior change for other configs.

  Not duplicating an existing PR: #47604 is a revert, not a fix; no other forward-fix is open.

  ## Test Plan

  - Repro script driving the real `_reshape_kv_cache()` with real DSV4-SWA / TurboQuant specs, run before and after the fix.
  - E2E of the #42890 feature: gpt-oss-20b, `kv_cache_dtype=nvfp4` + `kv_cache_dtype_skip_layers=["sliding_window"]`, FlashInfer, both v1/v2 model runners.
  - `ruff check` on touched files.

  ## Test Result

  - Before: Case A last dim **512** (FlashInfer expects 584); Case B raises `Unknown TurboQuant cache dtype: 'auto'`.
  - After: Case A → `(4, 64, 584)` ✅; Case B → `(4, 16, 8, 134)` (TQ slot layout) ✅. Verified fail→pass both directions via stash/pop.
  - E2E: both runners exit 0, coherent 2048-token greedy output, byte-identical v1 vs v2. Ruff clean.
  - Caveat: DSV4/SM121 verified at reshape-unit level (no SM121 hardware); would appreciate confirmation from the original reporter.

items.title: [Performance]: Triton and other eager attention backends re-derive K/V cache views on every call (same class as #59534)
items.body:
### Proposal to improve performance

#59534 reports that the FlashAttention backend re-derives its K/V cache views
(`kv_cache.transpose(1, 2).split(head_size, dim=-1)` + stride canonicalization)
on every attention call, although the views depend only on the `kv_cache`
tensor's storage/shape/strides, which are fixed once the cache is allocated.

The same per-call derivation exists in several other eager-path backends
(line numbers @ main `65ff14056`):

| Backend | Call sites | Extra per-call work |
|---|---|---|
| `triton_attn.py` | L655, L744, L828, L863 | FP8 KV adds two `view(fp8_dtype)` retypes per call |
| `flex_attention.py` | L1233, L1346–1348 | — |
| `hpc_attn.py` | L443 | — |
| `rocm_aiter_fa.py` | L1666 | — |
| `flash_attn_diffkv.py` | L111, L193 | — |
| `flashinfer.py` (trtllm path) | L2839, L2844 | — |

`TritonAttentionImpl` already caches its KV **scale** views
(`_k_scale_cache` / `_v_scale_cache`, triton_attn.py L411–475) and clears them
in the profiling cleanup, so caching the K/V **data** views per `kv_cache`
tensor identity fits the backend's existing design directly.

### Measurements

Host time per call (RTX 5090, torch 2.14.0+cu132, main @ `4e0ad5720`,
N=2000 iters after warmup, bf16 cache, blocks=1000/block=16/hd=128):

| Derivation | num_kv_heads=1 | =4 | =8 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Triton decoder: `transpose+split` | 5.44 µs | 5.30 µs | 5.23 µs |
| Triton FP8 path: `transpose+split+2x view(fp8)` | 7.23 µs | 6.97 µs | 7.10 µs |
| Cached-view hit (the FA fix from #59534, for scale) | 0.12 µs | 0.13 µs | 0.12 µs |

Like #59534, this is host time on the critical path wherever attention runs
eagerly (prefill / mixed batches under the default `FULL_AND_PIECEWISE`), and
it multiplies by `num_layers` per step. The FP8-KV Triton path pays the retype
on top. (The Triton backend is the default on ROCm and a common fallback
elsewhere, so the affected population is not small.)

### Proposed fix

Cache the derived views per `kv_cache` tensor identity on the impl, exactly as
#64571 (the FA fix for #59534) does (`_get_kv_views` keyed on tensor identity,
rebuilt when the profiling cache is replaced by the real one). For Triton, the
cached entry can also hold the FP8-retyped variants so the quantized path skips
the per-call `view(fp8_dtype)` as well.

I'm happy to open the PR(s) — either per-backend or one change over the shared
helper, whichever maintainers prefer.

### Your current environment

```text
OS                : Ubuntu 24.04.5 LTS (x86_64)
GPU               : NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5090 (sm_120)
Nvidia driver     : 595.91.07
PyTorch version   : 2.14.0+cu132
Python version    : 3.12.3
```

items.body:
## Summary

Harden the native NVFP4 KV-cache writer test with a relative-L2 error bound of 0.15, and make its V-scale reference match the native writer on SM120. This changes tests only.

Rebased onto `main` at `d15be0856d` on 2026-10-30. Main already has the shared dequantizer's `swizzled_scales` option, so the remaining change is confined to `tests/kernels/attention/test_cache.py`.

## Why this matters

The native `reshape_and_cache_nvfp4_dispatch` writer in `csrc/nvfp4_kv_cache_kernels.cu` stores K scales linearly and V scales in the 4x4 swizzle on every supported architecture. Main's test had selected linear V scales on SM120, conflating that native writer with FlashInfer's separate cache-update path. The reference now follows the native writer actually invoked by this test.

The relative-L2 bound supplements the existing elementwise check; neither tolerance is loosened. This catches structurally wrong scale ordering.

## Validation

RTX 5090 / SM120, Python 3.12, PyTorch 2.13.0+cu130. Reused the prior precompiled native extension. Its corresponding NVFP4 writer source differs from this base only in three include paths after the shared-header move; no native kernel modification is included in this PR.

```bash
# 24 passed, 264 skipped, 1008 deselected

.venv/bin/python -m pre_commit run --files tests/kernels/attention/test_cache.py
```
