items.title: [CuTe] Speed up SM100 hdim-64 bwd: dedicated P/dS TMEM slots + per-warp signaling
items.body:
Two coupled changes to the hdim-64 SM100 backward that together remove every compute-wide barrier from its main loop. Gradients are bit-identical to the current kernel under `deterministic=True`; every other shape and architecture is untouched.

**Results** (B200, bf16, 64k tokens per call, 32 query heads, sustained-load medians, shipped default vs current main):

| shape | mode | before, TFLOP/s | after, TFLOP/s | speed-up |
|---|---|--:|--:|--:|
| b2 s32k h32:32 | dense | 731 | 841 | 1.150x |
| b2 s32k h32:32 | causal | 705 | 808 | 1.147x |
| b4 s16k h32:8 | dense | 840 | 903 | 1.075x |
| b4 s16k h32:8 | causal | 750 | 842 | 1.123x |
| b8 s8k h32:32 fp16 | dense | 692 | 782 | 1.131x |
| b4 s16k h32:32 | dense, deterministic | 709 | 774 | 1.091x |
| b4 s16k h32:32 | causal, deterministic | 664 | 725 | 1.093x |

Every measured hdim-64 shape improves by 6-15%, and the gain grows with sequence length. A 124-configuration sweep (seqlen 512 to 32k, MHA/GQA/MQA, dense, causal, local, varlen, bf16/fp16, deterministic and not) gives a geometric-mean speed-up of **1.129x non-deterministic** (worst cell 1.023x) and **1.050x deterministic** (worst cell 0.995x). hdim 128 is unchanged.

## Why the hdim-64 backward is slow

At hdim 64 the 1-CTA backward only uses TMEM columns [0, 384), and the bf16 P and dS tiles the compute warps write are aliased over the fp32 S and dP accumulators. Because each warp may only touch its own 32-lane sector, and the eight compute warps span two warpgroups, warp w's P store lands under warp w+4's S lanes. The kernel therefore guards each overwrite with a compute-wide named barrier (an "alias guard"): one for P over S, two for dS over dP. Two more compute-wide barriers sit in front of the signals the compute warps send after their stores. Five barriers per tile hold all eight warps to the pace of the slowest, and the aliasing also forces the MMA warp to wait for PV_t before it can issue QK_{t+1}, so the tensor core idles through most of the softmax.

## What changes

**1. Dedicated TMEM slots for P and dS (`split_P_dS`).** P moves to columns [384, 448) and dS to [448, 512). With nothing aliased:
- the alias guards have nothing to guard and are removed; the per-warp `tcgen05.wait::ld` in front of each stays, since each warp still has to wait for its own asynchronous TMEM loads;
- the fused "S read and P written" handshake splits in two: `pipeline_S_P` now carries only "S read", signalled as soon as S is in registers, and a new one-stage `pipeline_P` carries "P written" / "P consumed";
- the MMA warp issues QK_{t+1} on "S read" alone, ahead of PV_t. Its issue order becomes `QK_{t+1}, PV_t, dK_t, dQ_t, dP_{t+1}`, so the next S tile is computed under the current softmax.

**2. Per-warp signaling (`warp_sync`).** The three remaining compute-wide barriers each sit in front of an mbarrier that already expects one arrival per compute warp, so the barrier was redundant convergence. Each is replaced by `sync_warp`; the mbarrier is the cross-warp join. This is only legal once the alias guards are gone, which is why the two ship together.

Both knobs are in the JIT cache key and default to on wherever legal (1-CTA, 128x128 tiles, hdim 64). `split_P_dS=False, warp_sync=False` reproduces the original control flow exactly, which is what makes the differential tests below possible. `warp_sync` is asserted off at 2-CTA: there the dS/dPsum site's barrier orders the compute warps' `sdS_xchg` writes before a single-thread DSMEM copy to the peer CTA.

**Ablation** (each change alone vs both, sustained load): dedicated slots alone are worth about 2% on dense and 3-4% on causal shapes; per-warp signaling alone is worth 8-9% on dense and roughly nothing on causal, because the alias guards inside the dS stage loop have to stay; together they are worth 13-15% on dense and 11-15% on causal. Most of the win is only reachable once the alias guards are gone.

## Correctness

Neither change alters arithmetic or reduction order, so with `deterministic=True` dq/dk/dv are bit-identical to the current kernel. This was checked with a differential suite against the baseline knobs (`split_P_dS=False, warp_sync=False`), which reproduce the original control flow exactly: bit-exact comparison across dense, causal, GQA, local-window, varlen and odd/ragged sequence lengths, both iteration parities and `main_loop_iters == 0`; the same oracle under SM contention, an occupancy sweep and interleaved launches; a subprocess liveness watchdog; and differential `compute-sanitizer` runs with no new report attributable to the change. The suite's sensitivity was measured rather than assumed: sabotage mutants that re-alias the TMEM regions with the barriers removed are each caught within seconds. Static checks confirm the dealiasing introduces no new TMEM overlap and that every barrier weakened to `sync_warp` fronts an mbarrier expecting one arrival per compute warp. On the non-deterministic path, max error against an fp32 reference matches the baseline everywhere.

The hdim-64 subsets of `test_flash_attn.py` and `test_flash_attn_varlen.py` pass on a B200 with no new failures.

**Measurement.** Per-iteration CUDA events over back-to-back call trains, arms interleaved with rotating order, median of kept iterations; clocks unlocked, so the trains ride the power cap, which is the training-representative regime.

items.title: [Cute, Sm100] 1CTA MLA forward (dense + sparse top-k), MLA dispatch heuristic, sparse MLA backward at any head count
items.body:
This PR adds new 1CTA MLA kernels adapted for dense decode or sparse top-k with <= 64 query heads, and extends recompute P sparse MLA backward to cover heads 1...128 via supporting the TMA padding introduced in #2883. The new 1CTA MLA forward kernel supports fp8 with descale tensors and split-kv, and a follow-up PR adding this functionality for 2CTA MLA is planned. To simplify the merge, interface changes were kept minimal to the greatest extent possible.

Sparse MLA backward for 128 heads also speeds up ~1.5x by adding `-O2` to the compile options, as measured for cutlass dsl 4.7.1 with cu13 libs. See the table on the `-O2` fix below for more comprehensive numbers.

The rest of the PR description is Claude's summary.

## Summary

This PR adds a second SM100 forward kernel for MLA (absorbed: `qv` with hdim_v 512, rope
hdim 64). It runs one 64-row tile per CTA (`tcgen05.mma.ws`) instead of one 128-row tile per
2-CTA cluster. A dispatch heuristic chooses between it and the existing 2CTA kernel.

- **Dense MLA decode.** With split-KV, 1.1-22x faster than the 2CTA kernel (largest at small
  batch and long context). The 2CTA kernel cannot split at hdim_v 512. Large-batch decode
  reaches about 6.9 TB/s effective KV bandwidth.
- **Sparse (top-k) MLA, up to 64 Q heads.** 1.6-1.8x on prefill and 1.1-1.3x on large-batch
  decode. The 64-head training step is 1.10x faster with the same recompute-P backward.
- **Sparse MLA training below 64 heads.** The recompute-P backward now handles any head
  count 1..128. Training at 24 / 32 heads is 1.34x faster (30.2 -> 22.5 ms at 16K).
- **New for MLA:** fp8 with descales, and split-KV. The 2CTA MLA kernel supports neither. Paged
  KV, varlen and the learnable sink work on both kernels.

No new API arguments. MLA calls are routed automatically; `FLASH_ATTENTION_MLA_1CTA=1` / `0`
forces the 1CTA / 2CTA kernel.

Much of this builds on #2914 (Lequn Chen): the 64-key-block forward mainloop,
its gather producer and PTX helpers, and three backward changes. See "Credits".

## What changes for callers

- **Routing.** MLA calls previously always ran the 2CTA kernel. Now `_mla_1cta_route` decides:
  - **fp8, descales, or explicit `num_splits > 1`** -> 1CTA (2CTA supports none of these).
  - **Sparse, <= 64 heads** (training only with `gather_bwd_recompute_p=True`) -> 1CTA once
    the 2CTA kernel exceeds one wave (`2 x tokens x kv_heads > num_SMs`). Otherwise 2CTA.
  - **Dense with `num_splits=0`** (the split heuristic) -> 1CTA if its split heuristic gives
    enough splits: >= 2 on the 64-key-block mainloop, >= 5 on the 128-key one. Otherwise the
    unsplit rule below applies.
  - **Dense unsplit** -> 1CTA on decode shapes (`seqlen_q x heads_per_kv <= 64`) past one
    2CTA wave. Otherwise 2CTA, including all prefill.
  - **Varlen without a host `max_seqlen_q`:** the per-sequence length is bounded by `total_q`.
    That bound decides what a call can run (the unsplit decode check, the kb64 mainloop
    below 64 heads), while the CLC and fp8 S-ahead policies treat the length as unknown and
    keep their decode setting. The split heuristic counts tiles from the tokens, so
    single-token varlen decode gets split-KV on 1CTA with or without the host hint.
- **Numerics.** Where the 1CTA kernel runs the 128-key mainloop, its outputs are bitwise
  identical to the 2CTA kernel's. The 64-key-block (kb64) mainloop is not bitwise with 2CTA:
  it meets a bf16-rounding contract, with out / o_lo rel-L2 < 2e-3 and gradients < 5e-3. It is
  bitwise run to run.
- **New input checks for MLA:**
  - `num_splits > 1` with `gather_kv_indices` raises `ValueError`. Before, the 2CTA path
    silently ran unsplit.
  - Block sparsity with `qv` asserts. Neither MLA kernel reads it; before, it was ignored.
  - fp8 absorbed MLA requires `k_descale` and `v_descale` to be the same tensor. Q@K^T and
    Qv@V^T share one accumulator, so one descale folds into the softmax scale. The check is
    tensor identity, not equal values, because comparing values would sync the device.
    Without a rope part (`q = k = None`), the latent cache's descale is `v_descale`; a
    `k_descale` that is not the same tensor raises instead of being ignored.
  - A caller's `out` with `head_dim_v == 512` must be 32-B aligned (it was 16 B), checked at
    allocation on every route, since the kb64 mainloop stores O 256 bits at a time.
    Buffers the interface allocates already are.
- **Recompute-P backward** (`gather_bwd_recompute_p=True`) now accepts any head count 1..128.
  It used to require 64 or 128.

## Kernels

**Forward: `flash_fwd_mla_1cta_sm100.py` (the 128-key mainloop).**
- Dense and sparse top-k gather; varlen Q / K; `seqused`; paged KV at any page size (TMA when
  `page_size == tile_n`, else a cp.async gather warp group).
- `pack_gqa` at any ratio; split-KV (fp32 partials with the existing combine kernel); fp8
  with descales; learnable sink.
- Q is held in TMEM. Sparse Q heads are padded to the 64-row tile in-kernel, through
  `pack_gqa.qheads_first_tma_view`.

**Forward: `flash_fwd_mla_1cta_kb64_sm100.py` (64-key blocks; subclass).**
- Serves 16-bit calls with <= 64 heads: sparse at any such count, and dense at 64 heads, or
  on decode with fewer.
- Three 64-key latent stages that stream in parts, so S starts behind the fill.
- Two front ends: a cp.async gather (sparse, and pages that are not a multiple of 64) and TMA
  (dense). The page size is a run-time value, so each loader is one binary for every page
  size.
- Split-KV with at least 4 key blocks per split; 256-bit O stores; packed varlen scheduling
  for dense; CLC on sparse and on dense prefill.
- A port of #2914's 64-head sparse forward mainloop into the 1CTA kernel, extended to dense
  (TMA and paged front ends, split-KV) and to fewer than 64 heads. The design record is
  `AI/SPARSE_MLA_1CTA.md`.

**Sparse MLA backward: `flash_bwd_mla_sm100.py` and new `flash_bwd_mla_dq_dqv_sm100_h64.py`.**
- At 64 heads, three changes ported from #2914 (`AI/SPARSE_MLA_64H.md`):
  - the dV accumulator hand-off is pipelined;
  - dK_rope is fused into the recompute-P main kernel;
  - a 1-CTA 64-row dQ/dQv kernel with a whole-row gather.
- Recompute-P at padded head counts:
  - Q_rope and the QvB copy of Qv load through padded heads-first TMA views;
  - padded `lse_log2` columns are +inf, so P = 0 exactly in the padded rows;
  - the 64-row dQ/dQv kernel covers 1..64 heads, with output bitwise equal to the generic
    kernel.
- The 64 / 128-head gradients are unchanged: dq / dqv bitwise, dk / dv within the kernel's
  atomic run-to-run noise.

## Performance (GB300, 152 SMs, bf16, cold L2 unless noted)

**Dense decode, 64 heads** (the 2CTA kernel cannot split at hdim_v 512):

| shape | 2CTA | 1CTA kb64 (split-KV) | speedup |
|---|---|---|---|
| b=1, s_k 8K / 32K / 128K | 0.103 / 0.326 / 1.312 ms | 0.024 / 0.035 / 0.059 ms | 4.4 / 9.4 / 22x |
| b=8, s_k 8K / 32K / 128K | 0.096 / 0.337 / 1.272 | 0.034 / 0.075 / 0.200 | 2.8 / 4.5 / 6.4x |
| b=128, s_k 8K / 32K | 0.228 / 0.823 | 0.196 / 0.696 | 1.16 / 1.18x |
| b=512, s_k 8K / 32K | 0.789 / 3.111 | 0.732 / 2.795 | 1.08 / 1.11x |

- kb64 saturates at about 6.9 TB/s effective KV bandwidth, the device-to-device copy rate.
- At 128 heads (the 128-key mainloop), 1CTA split is 1.2-6x faster than 2CTA up to batch 16.
- Dense prefill stays on 2CTA (1CTA runs 0.78-0.82x of it).

**Sparse, 64 heads, topk 2048:**

| shape | 2CTA / 1CTA kb64 |
|---|---|
| prefill s_q 4096 | 1.64-1.76x |
| decode b = 128 / 512 | 1.12-1.32x / 1.08-1.21x |
| decode b <= 32 | 0.77-0.92x (stays on 2CTA via the one-wave rule) |

**Sparse training step** (16K tokens, b = 1, one causal document, topk 2048, token chunk 4096;
forward + backward, all columns from one benchmark). Below 64 heads, recompute-P was
unavailable before this PR, so 2CTA load-P was the only route. **Before numbers taken after the `-O2` fix below.**

| heads | 2CTA fwd + load-P (before) | 2CTA fwd + recompute-P | 1CTA kb64 fwd + recompute-P |
|---|---|---|---|
| 64 | 29.27 ms | 25.89 | **23.46** |
| 32 | 30.40 | 25.08 | **22.71** |
| 24 | 30.22 | 24.88 | **22.49** |

**Sparse MLA backward: ptxas `-O2` instead of the default level.** At the ptxas default the
backward kernels spill heavily, the dQ/dQv GEMM about 4 KB of local memory per thread; at
`-O2` they spill 0-64 B. The level is now a per-kernel class attribute (`ptxas_options`). The
backward speedup below comes from the compiler level alone, not from the kernel changes in
this PR, and applies to 128 heads (all load-P and 2CTA training at 65-128 heads):

| heads, tokens, mode | default -> `-O2`, backward total | dQ/dQv | main kernel |
|---|---|---|---|
| 128, 16K, load-P | 43.99 -> 29.35 ms (**1.50x**) | 18.88 -> 4.58 ms (4.1x) | 19.30 -> 19.13 |
| 128, 16K, recompute-P | 48.97 -> 30.97 ms (**1.58x**) | 19.03 -> 4.58 ms (4.2x) | 24.24 -> 20.87 |
| 128, 4K, load-P | 10.34 -> 7.03 ms (1.47x) | 4.37 -> 1.14 ms (3.8x) | 4.60 -> 4.54 |
| 128, 4K, recompute-P | 11.55 -> 7.41 ms (1.56x) | 4.38 -> 1.14 ms (3.8x) | 5.84 -> 4.96 |
| 64, 16K, load-P / recompute-P | 1.36x / 1.37x | 3.0x | 1.01x / 1.04x |
| 24, 16K, load-P | 1.34x | 3.0x | 1.00x |

GB300, b = 1, causal, topk 2048, per-kernel CUDA time from the profiler. Two GPUs with opposite
run orders agree to within 1%. The backward total also includes the preprocess (unchanged)
and the dK GEMM (1.04x). The 64 / 24-head rows predate the 64-row dQ/dQv kernel and the fused
dK_rope, which now replace those kernels at up to 64 heads. The forward kernels gain as well:
the sparse forward median is +15-17% at `-O2` on both 2CTA and the 128-key 1CTA mainloop; the
kb64 mainloop stays at the default level, where `-O2` is 7-8% slower.

**Dispatch accuracy.** With the variable unset and `num_splits=0`, the auto route is within 1%
of the faster kernel on every benchmarked dense shape, measured both cold and with CUDA graphs.
The one exception is the 128-head, b=24, s_k=8K boundary case, at 1.05-1.06x.

Details: `AI/SPARSE_MLA_1CTA.md` ("Performance" and "Dispatch heuristic");
benchmark: `benchmarks/benchmark_sparse_mla_fwd.py`.

## Fixes to existing paths

- **`DescaleTensors` (all SM100 fp8 forwards).** Partial descales arrived shifted inside the
  kernel. `__new_from_mlir_values__` refilled the members that were present from the left, so
  a lone `v_descale` became `q_descale`: it scaled QK instead of O, a max error of 1.58 on a
  unit-scale test. `k` + `v` became `q` + `k`. The members are now rebuilt by which ones were
  present. A new regression test covers every subset.
- **JIT disk cache.** Export is now atomic (temp file + `os.replace`). An unloadable entry is
  treated as a miss instead of an error, and the export replaces it even when it is nonempty
  (a truncated object from an interrupted write). Before, a full disk left zero-byte objects
  that failed every later load, and a truncated one was recompiled by every process.
- **Paged `max_seqlen_k`** defaults to the page-table row (`page_size x page_table.shape[1]`)
  for every paged call, not the pool size. That is the kernels' own static key length. The
  pool size over-split small calls, e.g. 6 splits over 2 key blocks; outside MLA it only
  feeds the split heuristic.

### Paged KV: the padding contract, and empty sequences on TMA KV loads

When pages load by TMA (a page holds whole key tiles: `page_size == tile_n`, or for the kb64
mainloop any multiple of 64), a tile loads every row of its key block. That includes rows past
`seqused_k` in a sequence's last, partially used page. Their scores are masked, so P = 0 there,
but `0 x NaN = NaN` in P @ V. The contract, now in the `page_table` docstring and at the kb64
TMA page load:

- **Rows past `seqused_k` in a partially used page must be finite.** Their values do not
  matter. This holds on every TMA page path (MLA and the regular kernel, as on main); cp.async
  paths zero-fill those rows.
- **Pages a sequence does not use may hold anything,** NaN included, also for a sequence with
  `seqused_k = 0`.

The second half did not hold before this PR, on any TMA path, main's regular SM100 forward
included. A sequence with `seqused_k = 0` still runs one fully masked dummy block, which loads a
tile from its first page-table entry, a page it does not use. A NaN there reached O: the
epilogue scaled the accumulator by 0, and `NaN x 0` stays NaN. With split-KV the empty split
is skipped, so only unsplit calls were affected.

**Fix:** with TMA KV loads and `seqlen_k == 0`, the epilogue writes zeros instead of scaling
the accumulator:
- the regular SM100 forward: `correction_epilogue`'s `zero_fill` now also takes a run-time
  flag; the block-sparse empty-tile path stays compile time;
- the 2CTA, 128-key 1CTA and kb64 MLA forwards.

It adds one tile-uniform branch per output chunk (not separately benchmarked) and folds away
at compile time on cp.async paths.

Measured before the fix (bf16, one sequence with `seqused_k = 0` whose first page is NaN,
unsplit): every TMA route (kb64 pages 64 / 128, the 128-key mainloop at page 128, 2CTA, and
the regular kernel at head dims 64 / 128) returned NaN for that sequence. After the fix, all
return O = 0 and LSE = -inf.

**Tests:** `test_flash_attn_mla_paged_padding_contract` (7 MLA routes) and
`test_flash_attn_paged_padding_contract` (regular kernel: head dims 128 / 64, pages 128 / 64,
split and unsplit). Each covers a NaN-filled unused page and large finite garbage in the unused
tail. The output must equal the zero-padding run bitwise, with O = 0 and LSE = -inf for empty
sequences.

## Interface

- `_get_fwd_config` and its call site are unchanged from main. The only exception: MLA calls
  pass `num_splits=1`.
- `max_seqlen_q` / `max_seqlen_k` are normalized before the MLA route, so routing and planning
  read the same values.
- The MLA planning is in `_mla_fwd_plan`. It picks the kernel class and the 1CTA tile and split
  count, and routes again when the auto split is too small.
- Kernel-specific choices live on the kernel classes: `ptxas_options`, `can_implement`,
  `use_clc`, `use_s_ahead`, `TILE_MN`, `MIN_BLOCKS_PER_SPLIT`.
- **Forward compile key** vs main:
  - added the route: `mla_1cta`, `mla_1cta_kb64`, and fp8 S-ahead;
  - `qhead_per_kvhead` removed, since the sparse padded width follows from `nheads_per_kv`
    and the route;
  - `paged_kv_tma` replaces the paged-non-TMA flag, carrying the same information for the
    other kernels;
  - the 1CTA CLC policy goes into the existing `use_clc_scheduler` entry.
- `FLASH_ATTENTION_MLA_1CTA` is the only new environment variable.
- `cute_dsl_utils.assume_strides_aligned` / `assume_tensor_aligned` take an `align_bits`
  argument, used for the 256-bit O stores.

## Testing

- **MLA tests** moved to `tests/cute/test_flash_attn_mla.py`, about 2.3K cases; that file
  collects in about 2 s. `test_flash_attn.py` went from about 418K cases (15 s per worker to
  collect) to what remains.
- **Every MLA test supports the two-pass flow.** The compile pass runs under FakeTensorMode at
  high `-n`; the execution pass runs from the disk cache.
- **New conftest instrumentation** (documented in `CLAUDE.md`):
  - `FLASH_ATTENTION_TEST_EXPECT_CACHED=1` fails any test that compiles during the execution
    pass;
  - `FLASH_ATTENTION_TEST_COUNT_COMPILES`;
  - `FLASH_ATTENTION_TEST_RECORD_KEYS[_ONLY]`, for diffing the compiled kernel set across
    changes.
- `tools/two_pass_tests.sh -k EXPR -g GPUS [-f FILES]` runs both passes.
- The suite pins `FLASH_ATTENTION_MLA_1CTA=0` by default. Rerun with `=1` to cover the 1CTA
  kernel. The dispatch tests unset the variable themselves.

- `tools/two_pass_tests.sh` keeps both passes on the `-g` GPUs. The compile pass does no GPU
  work, but each worker opens a CUDA context.

The full MLA test suite was ran two-pass with the flag at 0 and at 1, and all tests passed.

## Credits

From PR #2914, by Lequn Chen:
- the 64-key-block (H64) sparse forward mainloop, ported into the 1CTA kernel as the kb64
  mainloop;
- `CpasyncGatherKVManagerH64` (`topk_gather_kv.py`), the whole-row gather used by the kb64
  forward and the 64-row dQ/dQv kernel;
- the `tcgen05` PTX helpers the kb64 mainloop uses (`blackwell_helpers.py`:
  `gemm_ws_ts_ptx_partial`, `utccp_128x256b_ptx`, `tcgen05_fence_after_thread_sync`);
- the three 64-row backward changes: the pipelined dV accumulator hand-off, dK_rope fused
  into the recompute-P main kernel, and the 1-CTA 64-row dQ/dQv kernel (commits authored by
  Lequn Chen).

## Map of the code

| area | files |
|---|---|
| 1CTA forward, 128-key mainloop | `flash_fwd_mla_1cta_sm100.py`, `blackwell_helpers.py` (`gemm_ws_ts_ptx_partial`, `utccp_128x256b_ptx`, `cp_smem_to_tmem_dup_64`) |
| 1CTA forward, kb64 mainloop | `flash_fwd_mla_1cta_kb64_sm100.py`, `topk_gather_kv.py` (`CpasyncGatherKVManagerH64`, paged mode) |
| Sparse backward | `flash_bwd_mla_sm100.py`, `flash_bwd_mla_dq_dqv_sm100_h64.py`, `pack_gqa.py` |
| Routing and planning | `interface.py`: `_mla_1cta_route`, `_mla_fwd_plan` |
| Fixes | `flash_fwd_sm100.py` (`DescaleTensors`), `cache_utils.py` |
| Tests and tooling | `tests/cute/test_flash_attn_mla.py`, `tests/cute/conftest.py`, `tools/two_pass_tests.sh` |
| Design notes | `AI/SPARSE_MLA_1CTA.md`, `AI/SPARSE_MLA_64H.md`, `AI/SPARSE_MLA_RECOMPUTE_P.md` |

## Known limitations and follow-ups

- **Sparse MLA has no split-KV** on either kernel.
- **Sparse above 64 heads, and sparse training with load-P,** run on 2CTA.
- **Dense kb64 does not cover** more than 64 heads, fp8, or dense prefill below 64 heads. These
  run the 128-key mainloop.
- **Small-batch sparse decode** stays on 2CTA, which is faster there. The 1CTA per-block latency
  on one SM is the limit; candidates are listed in `AI/SPARSE_MLA_1CTA.md`, "Limitations and follow-ups".
- **The dispatch thresholds were measured on GB300 (152 SMs).** The one-wave rule scales with
  the SM count; the split thresholds (2 / 5) may need retuning on other parts.

items.title: [CuTe,Bwd,Sm100] Support head_dim not a multiple of 32 in backward
items.body:
## Summary

Backward on SM100 (B200/B300) crashes or **silently produces wrong dK/dV** when `head_dim % 32 != 0` (e.g. ViT `head_dim=72`, `104`). Fixes #2492. Three independent root causes:

1. **`flash_bwd_preprocess.py`** — the O/dO load predicate (`predicate_k`) carries a `CPY_M` mode broadcast over `m`, but the copy source is sliced per-`m` (`tOgO[None, m, None]`) without slicing the predicate. The vectorized 128-bit copy atom's predicate-shape verifier then rejects the extra mode (`expects (1,(k)) but got (1,(cpy_m,k))`). Slice the predicate per-`m`, as `flash_fwd.py` / `flash_bwd.py` already do.

2. **`flash_bwd_sm100.py`** — `tile_hdim` padded `head_dim` to a multiple of 16, but the dQ accumulator reduce requires a multiple of 32 (`assert tile_hdim % dQ_reduce_ncol == 0`), and both the preprocess kernel and the interface already round to 32. `head_dim=72 -> 80` tripped the assert. Pad to 32 so all three agree (96); this reuses the already-working `head_dim=96` path.

3. **`interface.py`** — varlen MHA uses the non-TMA dK/dV epilogue store, which writes `tile_hdim` (mult of 32) columns per row with no head-dim OOB predication (its 16-wide vectorization cannot mask a 72 boundary). It spilled past the real `head_dim` and corrupted neighboring dK/dV. Route that store through a head-dim-padded scratch buffer, then slice back. Gated on `arch // 10 in [10, 11]` so SM90/SM120 skip the extra alloc + copy (suggested by @hebo1221).

## Test results

Validated on **B300 (SM103)** against `torch.nn.functional.scaled_dot_product_attention` (fp32 reference):

- **Coverage**: dense + varlen, causal + non-causal, `head_dim ∈ {64, 72, 80, 104, 128}`, MHA and GQA(hd=128).
- **Result**: `dq/dk/dv` max relative error **2e-3 – 7e-3** (bf16 precision), matching the multiple-of-32 baselines. No regression on aligned head dims.
- **End-to-end**: Qwen3.5-VL training (ViT `head_dim=72`, varlen) trains with a decreasing loss and finite grad norm.

## Relation to #2633

This is an alternative to #2633. #2633 keeps V padding at a multiple of 16 and predicates the non-TMA store via a reduced tmem `Repetition` — neater for varlen. However, in our testing that leaves the **dense (TMA-store) dV path numerically wrong** for `head_dim % 32 != 0` (relative error ~1–13 on `dv` for hd 72/80/104), while the varlen path is correct. Padding V to 32 keeps **both dense and varlen** paths correct, at the cost of a little extra dV compute. Happy to combine approaches if maintainers prefer the leaner store.

## Test plan
- [x] Numerical parity vs SDPA (fp32 ref), dense + varlen, causal + non-causal, hd {64,72,80,104,128}
- [x] No regression on multiple-of-32 head dims
- [x] End-to-end VLM training smoke (ViT hd=72)
- [ ] Maintainer CI matrix

## Acknowledgments

Thanks to @hebo1221 for independently verifying all three fixes via FakeTensor compilation on SM121 and for pointing out that the scratch-buffer path should be gated to SM100/SM110 only.

items.title: [CuTe, SM100] Support 1..128 Q heads in sparse MLA via in-kernel TMA padding
items.body:
## Human Note

Support [1, 128] Q heads in the public sparse MLA (DSA) forward and backward paths. I saw that there was a comment for supporting n_qheads = 64 not sure if you planned to do something fancier here. I did the easy thing (just pad out).  This does infact come up both for dsv4 flash and when doing tp sharding. I found this when trying to integrate into torchtitan. I consider this a naive unblock but it does help :)


I thought about the multi tokens e.g. true pack-gqa but didnt want to visit the union + masking (although ill prototype this) -> same reason why I didnt support this for blocksparse impl

## Agent Notes
TMA pads heads inside the kernel without padded operand copies in global memory. This enables training with 64-head models and tensor-parallel shards.

Each forward tile still covers one token and one top-k gather list: 2-CTA UMMA, 128 packed Q heads, 64 rows per CTA, with K/V split across the pair. Backward uses a 64- or 128-head tile. The dQ/dQv GEMM keeps its 128-row tile with a dynamic head extent.

Unchanged: attention math, the 128-head TMA path, MMA tile sizes, and pipeline synchronization.

### Mechanism

- `padded_qheads_tma_source` builds a heads-first view `(h, d, s, b)` with a dynamic head extent, so CuTe tiles it without requiring divisibility. TMA zero-fills out-of-bounds loads and drops out-of-bounds stores. `regroup_padded_qheads` restores the packed coordinate layout `((tile, s), d, 1, b)`.
- LSE, row_max, and learnable-sink accesses guard the packed head index. Without guards, the hierarchical packed layout wraps padded heads into the next token.
- TMA loads zero padded Q rows in forward and dO/P rows in backward. These rows produce `dS = 0` and contribute nothing to dK/dV. Only `scaleP`/`dPsum` need tile-width global buffers with finite padding.

### Two latent bugs

1. **Backward dV staging at `tile_m=64`.** The split-0 epilogue could overwrite dOt/Qvt operands still used by the split-1 MMA, producing NaNs in `dV[:, 256:]`. If staging equals one operand stage, each split now stages in place over its consumed stage. Otherwise, both splits take turns using one staging area allocated after the operands.
2. **Non-power-of-two preprocess tiles.** A 48-row tile (2 tokens × 24 heads) produced incorrect `dpsum`. Padded head counts now use trivial packing (`qhead_per_kvhead=1, nheads_kv=H`) with the existing 128-row tile. Not all head counts divide that tile; resizing it to a non-power-of-two is not a valid workaround.

### Validation (GB200)

- Sentinel-focused run: 44 passed. `test_flash_attn_mla_sparse_bwd_sentinel` covers H ∈ {128, 64, 96, 24, 1} × shared_kv × causal × 2 lengths.
- `test_flash_attn_mla_absorbed`: 96 BF16 cases passed for `1024-1024` and `255-1025`, including the 128-head path.
- Probe against global-memory padding to 128 heads, H ∈ {1, 8, 16, 24, 48, 64, 72, 96, 100, 120}: out/LSE/P/row_max/dQ/dQv bit-identical; dK/dV within 1e-5.

### Performance at DeepSeek-V4 shapes

Measurement contract: GB200, B=1, D_qk = D_v = 512, shared KV, sliding window 128 + compressed causal top-k, via attention-gym `selected_attention`. Flash uses top-k 512; pro uses top-k 1024. Times are medians over CUDA-graph replays, in µs per call (lower is better). Peak memory is MB (lower is better).

Calculated rates (higher is better): fwd FLOPs = 2*T*H*K*(D_qk + D_v), K = valid gathered slots (top-k + window); bwd FLOPs = 2.5× fwd. TB/s counts gathered KV rows plus Q read and O write.

| T | config | fwd us | fwd TFLOPS | fwd TB/s | bwd us | bwd TFLOPS | fwd+bwd us | peak MB |
|---:|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 4096 | flash H=64 in-kernel pad | 859 | 400 | 3.75 | 1874 | 458 | 2733 | 2114 |
| 4096 | flash H=64 gmem pad->128 | 1061 | 324 | 3.04 | 2835 | 303 | 3896 | 4557 |
| 4096 | H=128, flash topk 512 | 918 | 749 | 4.10 | 2465 | 697 | 3382 | 4046 |
| 4096 | pro H=128 topk 1024 | 1349 | 917 | 4.38 | 3798 | 814 | 5147 | 5109 |
| 8192 | flash H=64 in-kernel pad | 1666 | 412 | 3.87 | 3702 | 464 | 5368 | 4095 |
| 8192 | H=128, flash topk 512 | 1775 | 774 | 4.24 | 4876 | 705 | 6651 | 7959 |
| 8192 | pro H=128 topk 1024 | 2650 | 933 | 4.46 | 7539 | 820 | 10189 | 10087 |
| 16384 | flash H=64 in-kernel pad | 3293 | 417 | 3.91 | 7347 | 468 | 10640 | 8061 |
| 16384 | H=128, flash topk 512 | 3506 | 784 | 4.29 | 9723 | 707 | 13229 | 15789 |
| 16384 | pro H=128 topk 1024 | 5262 | 940 | 4.49 | 15029 | 823 | 20292 | 20045 |

At T=4096, H=64 in-kernel padding reduces fwd+bwd time by about 30% and peak memory by about half versus global-memory padding. H=64 forward takes about 93% of the H=128 time. NCU on the H=64 forward (T=4096): DRAM throughput 8%, L2 hit rate 74%, 74% of stall cycles are long-scoreboard waits on the per-thread cp.async gather. The forward is gather-latency-bound, so the padded MMA rows cost little; the gather itself is the lever for a follow-up.

Separate T=2048 comparison: GB200, top-k 512, D=512, fwd+bwd via attention-gym `selected_attention`; time in µs per call (lower is better).

| Configuration | fwd+bwd us |
|---|---:|
| H=64 in-kernel padding | 1416 |
| Native H=128 | 1740 |
| H=64 gmem padding to 128 | 1979 |

items.title: fix(hd256/sm100): make the dedicated hd256 kernel stride-aware (supersede #2666 copy)
items.body: Fixes #2665. Supersedes the `.contiguous()` stop-gap from #2666. ## Summary The dedicated head_dim=256 SM100 (Blackwell) forward kernel built its q/k/v CuTe layouts with strides synthesized from shape assuming a fully-contiguous BSHD tensor) and reused only the input's base pointer. maybe_contiguous() in the interface only guarantees stride(-1) == 1, so a transpose(1, 2) -ed input — contiguous in the head dim but with swapped sequence/head strides — reached the kernel and produced TMA loads from the wrong addresses, silently corrupting outputs on B200 at `head_dim=256` (#2665). Other head dims and H100 were unaffected because they use kernels that already honor arbitrary input strides. #2666 worked around this by forcing q/k/v contiguous before the kernel, which adds a full copy (~0.4 GB for the issue's `1×32×8192×256` shape) on every forward in the common transposed-input case. **This PR makes the kernel honor the real input strides instead, so the copy is no longer needed.** ## Root cause python # before: strides synthesized from shape, base pointer reused q_layout = cute.make_layout( (s_q_total, d, ((h_r, h_k), b)), stride=(d64 * h_r64 * h_k64, 1, ((d64, d64 * h_r64), stride_b_qo)), # assumes contiguous ) q = cute.make_tensor(q_tensor.iterator, q_layout) This is consistent with how the **general** SM100 forward kernel (`flash_fwd_sm100.py`) and the **hd256 backward** kernels already work — both derive their layouts from the actual tensor strides. The hd256 forward was the only kernel still assuming contiguity. ## Changes - Forward (dense + paged): derive the sequence / head / batch strides from the actual q/k/v tensors for the rank-5, rank-4, and rank-3 (varlen) paths. The `d` (head_dim) mode is kept a **static `1`** — TMA requires the contiguous innermost mode's stride to be statically known, and `maybe_contiguous()` guarantees `stride(-1) == 1`. - Backward: the hd256 backward kernels already derive layouts from real strides, so #2666's backward .contiguous()` was redundant and is removed. - interface.py`: replace the unconditional copy with an **alignment-gated guard** (`maybe_hd256_compatible_contiguous`) that copies only when an input stride would violate the kernel's 16-byte / divby-64 TMA assumptions. This keeps the zero-copy fast path for the common case while staying safe for exotic (e.g. sliced/padded) strides. ## Validation (B200) | Check | Result | |--------|--------| | #2665 repro (transposed, `1×32×8192×256`) | max_abs_err `0.155` → **`4.9e-4`** | | Forward, transposed vs contiguous (same kernel), MHA/GQA/causal | **bit-exact `0.0`** | | Backward, transposed vs contiguous — `out`/`dq`/`dk`/`dv`, MHA/GQA/causal | **bit-exact `0.0`** | | Paged-KV, non-contiguous q (same kernel) | **bit-exact `0.0`** | | Padded-stride fallback (e.g. stride `(…, 257, 1)`) | guard fires, result correct | For a contiguous input the derived strides are arithmetically identical to the old synthesized ones, so the existing supported path is bit-identical to before. ## Test plan - pytest tests/cute/test_flash_attn.py` on the `d=256` slice (forward + backward): **240 passed, 648 skipped** (skips = feature combos hd256 doesn't support: softcap / learnable_sink / local). - ruff check flash_attn/cute/` — clean. - tests ran are summarized in the table below: - ## Notes Developed as two independent implementations that converged on the same design (including the non-obvious TMA static-`1` requirement) and cross-validated each other's results on separate B200s. ## Coauthor: Coauthor: @oattia

items.title: Add dropout support to CuTe DSL attention kernels
items.body:
Addresses #2436

## Summary

- Dropout for CuTe DSL forward and backward kernels: SM80, SM90, SM100, SM120
- Philox 4x32 PRNG via `quack.rounding.mul_wide_u32` with FA2-compatible 6-input keying
- `dropout_p` and `dropout_seed` parameters on `flash_attn_func` and `flash_attn_varlen_func`

## Implementation

Per-element Philox keyed on global (row, col) position with full 64-bit seed. Identical masks in forward and backward regardless of thread partitioning. Branchless mask application after softmax, before P→V GEMM (forward) and after P recomputation (backward).

**Keying layout:**
```
counter = (batch*nheads + head, 0, row, col)
key     = (seed_lo, seed_hi)
```

**Architecture-specific integration:**

| Arch | Forward | Backward |
|------|---------|----------|
| SM80/SM120 | `compute_one_n_block` | `compute_one_m_block` |
| SM90 | Closure threaded through mma pipeline | Closure through `mma_one_m_block` with `SdP_swapAB` |
| SM100 | `apply_dropout_mask_sm100` (TMEM layout) | Transpose handling for S^T = K @ Q^T |

SM100 uses a separate `apply_dropout_mask_sm100` because its softmax operates on TMEM-loaded data with a different layout than the standard MMA accumulator.

## Stress test results (SM121a)

| Test | Result |
|------|--------|
| 50-iteration training loop (B=2 S=1024 H=8 D=64, fwd+bwd) | All gradients finite |

items.title: [CuTe, SM100] Add kv_start for causal document masking without a BlockMask
items.body:
We train on packed sequences. Every row of a `(batch, seqlen)` batch holds several documents, and a token should only attend to earlier tokens of its own document. On SM100 we've been doing this with a document `mask_mod` plus a `BlockMask`, and at long context the BlockMask turned into a real cost. At 2M tokens it is 2 GiB and takes almost 6 seconds to build. That happens every step, because the document boundaries change with every batch.

A causal document mask is much simpler than what a BlockMask can describe, though. For query `i`, the visible keys are one contiguous range: from the start of its document up to `i`. That start position never goes down as `i` grows. So one int32 per query is enough to describe the whole mask. FA4 already supports a per-row left edge for local attention; it just computes the edge from the window size. This PR lets you pass the edge in directly:

```python
out = flash_attn_func(q, k, v, causal=True, kv_start=kv_start)  # kv_start: (batch, seqlen_q) int32
```

Query `i` in batch `b` attends key `j` when `kv_start[b, i] <= j <= i`. If you also pass `window_size=(left, 0)`, the window applies on top of that.

Getting `kv_start` from document ids is a `cummax`:

```python
pos = torch.arange(seqlen, device=doc_ids.device, dtype=torch.int32).expand_as(doc_ids)
is_first = torch.ones_like(doc_ids, dtype=torch.bool)
is_first[:, 1:] = doc_ids[:, 1:] != doc_ids[:, :-1]
kv_start = torch.where(is_first, pos, 0).cummax(dim=1).values
kv_start = torch.where(doc_ids == pad_id, pos + 1, kv_start).int()  # padding tokens see nothing
```

The short version, on a B200: compared to the BlockMask path, it's 1.2-3.3x faster in the forward and 1.2-2.7x faster in forward + backward, and the mask is 4 bytes per token. Compared to varlen, it's the same speed on long documents and up to 1.4x faster on short ones, and you keep the `(batch, seqlen, heads, dim)` layout. The details are below, split into the three comparisons we care about.

## 1. Compared to a BlockMask

The BlockMask path pays in three places.

First, the mask has to be built. `create_block_mask` with 256x128 blocks (what `test_mask_mod.py` uses on SM100) grows with the square of the sequence length: 8 MiB and 24 ms at 128k, 512 MiB and 1.5 s at 1M, 2 GiB and 5.9 s at 2M, with an 8 GiB peak while it builds. At 2M that's 8x longer than the attention forward + backward it's built for.

Second, every partially masked tile calls the `mask_mod` for each of its elements, and a document `mask_mod` reads two document ids per call. With many documents, a lot of tiles cross a boundary.

Third, block-sparse calls run as non-causal. The forward gets `StaticPersistentTileScheduler` instead of the LPT scheduler that causal and local attention get (`FA_LOG_LEVEL=1` shows which one runs).

`kv_start` avoids all three. The mask is the `kv_start` tensor itself. Each thread already owns one row of S on SM100, so the per-row left edge costs one load per row, and after that it's the same R2P bit masking local attention uses. It runs on the local path, so it gets the LPT scheduler too.

Speed and memory against sequence length. B=1, 32 query heads, 8 KV heads, head dim 128, bf16, document lengths drawn from an exponential distribution with mean 4096. Times are ms for forward + backward.

| S | docs | BlockMask | kv_start | speedup | BlockMask size / build time / build peak | kv_start size / build time | peak memory for the step, BlockMask / kv_start |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 8k | 1 | 2.36 | 1.81 | 1.30x | 33 KiB / 0.9 ms / 0.1 MiB | 32 KiB / 0.03 ms | 0.35 / 0.35 GiB |
| 16k | 3 | 4.67 | 3.11 | 1.50x | 130 KiB / 1.0 ms / 0.2 MiB | 64 KiB / 0.05 ms | 0.69 / 0.69 GiB |
| 32k | 13 | 6.46 | 4.01 | 1.61x | 515 KiB / 1.8 ms / 0.9 MiB | 128 KiB / 0.07 ms | 1.39 / 1.39 GiB |
| 64k | 19 | 16.0 | 10.5 | 1.52x | 2 MiB / 6.5 ms / 3.5 MiB | 256 KiB / 0.14 ms | 2.78 / 2.77 GiB |
| 128k | 28 | 53.3 | 38.8 | 1.37x | 8 MiB / 24 ms / 14 MiB | 512 KiB / 0.27 ms | 5.55 / 5.55 GiB |
| 256k | 75 | 76.5 | 52.7 | 1.45x | 32 MiB / 92 ms / 56 MiB | 1 MiB / 0.52 ms | 11.13 / 11.10 GiB |
| 512k | 127 | 175 | 122 | 1.43x | 128 MiB / 366 ms / 224 MiB | 2 MiB / 0.92 ms | 22.31 / 22.19 GiB |
| 1M | 247 | 364 | 258 | 1.41x | 512 MiB / 1.47 s / 1.5 GiB | 4 MiB / 1.8 ms | 44.88 / 44.38 GiB |
| 2M | 502 | 717 | 508 | 1.41x | 2 GiB / 5.87 s / 8 GiB | 8 MiB / 3.6 ms | 90.75 / 88.77 GiB |

The step peak doesn't include q, k, v and dout. The 2 GiB difference at 2M is the BlockMask itself. The `kv_start` build time is the snippet above, which can also run in the data loader. In the backward, `kv_start` also needs `q_end` (described below), another 4 bytes per token for the length of the call.

Shorter documents make the gap bigger. Same setup, mean document length 512:

| S | docs | BlockMask | kv_start | speedup |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 8k | 17 | 1.12 | 0.51 | 2.18x |
| 32k | 63 | 4.66 | 2.30 | 2.02x |
| 128k | 246 | 17.3 | 9.07 | 1.91x |
| 512k | 1050 | 67.7 | 36.1 | 1.87x |
| 1M | 1997 | 137 | 71.1 | 1.92x |
| 2M | 4096 | 272 | 140 | 1.94x |

Even with one document, which is plain causal attention, the BlockMask path is 1.22-1.31x slower (8k to 512k; 1.29x at 1M).

Batched shapes give the same picture. Forward / forward + backward in ms, 32 query heads, 8 KV heads, head dim 128:

| B x S | docs | BlockMask | kv_start | speedup |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 8 x 8k | 8 | 4.92 / 18.95 | 3.72 / 14.70 | 1.32x / 1.29x |
| 8 x 8k | 72 | 2.82 / 10.02 | 1.31 / 5.88 | 2.15x / 1.70x |
| 8 x 8k | 251 | 2.03 / 7.46 | 0.71 / 3.59 | 2.87x / 2.08x |
| 2 x 32k | 2 | 16.98 / 65.39 | 14.11 / 52.79 | 1.20x / 1.24x |
| 2 x 32k | 58 | 3.26 / 11.56 | 1.54 / 6.85 | 2.12x / 1.69x |
| 1 x 128k | 1 | 129.95 / 498.25 | 110.10 / 407.64 | 1.18x / 1.22x |
| 1 x 128k | 110 | 6.05 / 22.58 | 3.02 / 13.69 | 2.00x / 1.65x |
| 1 x 128k | 525 | 3.66 / 14.71 | 1.38 / 7.51 | 2.66x / 1.96x |

With 16 heads and head dim 64 it's 1.22-3.30x in the forward and 1.16-2.68x in forward + backward. With a 4096-token sliding window on top of the documents, it's 1.41-2.75x and 1.37-1.93x. The full tables are at the end.

I wanted to know how much of this is just the cost of the `mask_mod` call, so I also ran the BlockMask path with a 32-wide vectorized `mask_mod` (`__vec_size__ = 32`). It reads `kv_start` from an aux tensor and returns a bitmask, which is about as cheap as a `mask_mod` can get. It only exists for the forward. Forward ms:

| B x S | docs | BlockMask, scalar mask_mod | BlockMask, vectorized mask_mod | kv_start |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 8 x 8k | 27 | 3.43 | 2.57 | 2.05 |
| 8 x 8k | 251 | 2.03 | 0.91 | 0.71 |
| 2 x 32k | 58 | 3.26 | 2.06 | 1.54 |
| 1 x 128k | 1 | 129.95 | 128.18 | 110.10 |
| 1 x 128k | 525 | 3.66 | 1.74 | 1.38 |

So with many documents, most of the forward gap is the per-element mask. The remaining 1.2-1.4x is the scheduler, plus walking one contiguous range of key blocks instead of looking up block indices. With one document only the diagonal tiles get masked, so a cheaper `mask_mod` barely helps there, and the 1.18x is entirely structural.

The backward gain doesn't come from 2-CTA. With `FA_DISABLE_2CTA=1`, both paths run the 1-CTA backward, and `kv_start` is still 1.11-1.66x faster. I also tried 256-wide KV blocks, which is what lets the BlockMask backward use 2-CTA. That was slower in forward + backward than 128-wide blocks in all 24 batched configurations, because coarser blocks leave more partially masked tiles.

## 2. score_mod and the other FlexAttention options still work

`kv_start` only replaces the mask. `score_mod` / `score_mod_bwd`, `softcap` and `learnable_sink` work with it the same way they work with plain causal attention. `test_cute_score_mod_with_kv_start` runs the four backward `score_mod` pairs from `test_score_mod.py` and compares the forward and the gradients against torch `flex_attention` with the same `score_mod` and a document `mask_mod`. That makes it the same computation as the flex version, just without the BlockMask.

The speedup holds with a `score_mod` attached. Same `score_mod` on both paths, 32/8 heads, head dim 128:

| score_mod | B x S | docs | BlockMask | varlen | kv_start | kv_start vs BlockMask |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `times_two` | 8 x 8k | 72 | 2.97 / 8.60 | 1.20 / 5.70 | 1.20 / 5.48 | 2.48x / 1.57x |
| `times_two` | 1 x 128k | 37 | 13.51 / 42.67 | 8.19 / 32.30 | 8.02 / 33.45 | 1.68x / 1.28x |
| `times_two` | 1 x 128k | 255 | 4.81 / 15.29 | 2.01 / 10.57 | 1.91 / 9.78 | 2.51x / 1.56x |
| `rel_bias_clamped` | 8 x 8k | 69 | 9.07 / 16.99 | 1.90 / 7.15 | 1.80 / 6.95 | 5.03x / 2.45x |
| `rel_bias_clamped` | 1 x 128k | 37 | 30.57 / 60.53 | 8.67 / 29.87 | 8.27 / 29.26 | 3.69x / 2.07x |
| `rel_bias_clamped` | 1 x 128k | 253 | 11.79 / 24.27 | 2.69 / 11.28 | 2.89 / 10.37 | 4.07x / 2.34x |

Forward / forward + backward in ms. The gap gets bigger with `rel_bias_clamped`. I think part of the reason is that the BlockMask path passes the document ids as an aux tensor, and when aux tensors are present the SM100 forward applies the `score_mod` one element at a time instead of two at a time (the `score_vec_size` default in `flash_fwd_sm100.py`). `kv_start` doesn't need aux tensors, so it keeps the default. I didn't dig further than that.

The one thing you can't do is combine `kv_start` with a `mask_mod`; the interface rejects that. For a mask that isn't "document start up to `i`", `mask_mod` + BlockMask is still the way to go.

## 3. Compared to varlen

Varlen computes the same thing. You flatten the batch to `(total_tokens, heads, dim)`, put one sequence per document in `cu_seqlens`, and pass `max_seqlen`. That works, but `kv_start` is easier to live with for a few reasons.

The shape stays fixed. `kv_start` is always `(batch, seqlen)`, however many documents the batch has. `cu_seqlens` has one entry per document, so its shape changes from batch to batch, and building it takes a `nonzero`, which syncs with the host. We call this kernel from JAX, where every shape has to be static, and that's how we ended up here. It also helps with CUDA graphs. I captured the forward and backward with `kv_start` in a single CUDA graph, then replayed it on batches with 4, 17, 33, 141 and 495 documents, just copying the new `kv_start` into the captured buffer each time. With `deterministic=True`, the output and dQ matched eager bitwise on every replay. With varlen you'd have to pad `cu_seqlens` to a fixed document count and pin `max_seqlen`; I haven't tried whether that works.

Short documents are faster. Varlen pads every document to a full 128-row tile, while with `kv_start` one tile can cover several short documents. At mean document length 256 that makes `kv_start` 1.27-1.41x faster in forward + backward, and at 512 it's 1.03-1.11x. From about 1k tokens per document up, the two are within 4% of each other.

It uses less memory with many documents. Varlen's backward peak grows with the number of documents. At 2M tokens with 4096 documents, varlen peaks at 104.9 GiB and `kv_start` at 88.8 GiB.

Padding and windows are per token. A padding token gets `kv_start = i + 1` and contributes nothing, so you don't have to cut padding out of the batch. A sliding window is either folded into `kv_start` or passed as `window_size`.

Forward + backward in ms, varlen vs `kv_start`:

| setup | docs | varlen | kv_start | kv_start vs varlen |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 8 x 8k, mean 4096 | 27 | 8.68 | 8.62 | 1.01x |
| 8 x 8k, mean 256 | 251 | 5.03 | 3.59 | 1.40x |
| 2 x 32k, mean 256 | 253 | 5.04 | 3.61 | 1.40x |
| 1 x 128k, mean 4096 | 34 | 25.25 | 26.22 | 0.96x |
| 1 x 128k, mean 256 | 525 | 9.57 | 7.51 | 1.27x |
| 1 x 2M, mean 4096 | 502 | 506 | 508 | 1.00x |
| 1 x 2M, mean 512 | 4096 | 156 | 140 | 1.11x |

## What changed

`kv_start` runs on the existing local-attention path with `window_size_right=0`. The only new part is that each query row's left edge is read from memory instead of computed from a window.

In the kernels (SM100 forward and backward):

- `SeqlenInfoQK` holds this batch's row of `kv_start` in the forward, or `q_end` in the backward.
- `BlockInfo`: in the forward, `n_block_min` comes from `kv_start` of the tile's first row, so key blocks to the left of every row's document are never loaded. The split between unmasked and left-masked blocks uses the tile's last row, so blocks every row can see run without masking. In the backward, `m_block_max` comes from `q_end` of the tile's last key. When there's also a `window_size_left`, the tighter bound wins.
- `mask.py`: the forward takes `max(window edge, kv_start[row])` as the left edge of each row. The backward's transposed mask gets the matching per-key limit from `q_end`.
- The deterministic backward also walks the m-blocks past `q_end` to signal the dQ semaphore, as it already does for local windows.

In the interface:

- `flash_attn_func` and `_flash_attn_fwd` take `kv_start`, and `_flash_attn_bwd` takes `q_end`. The autograd function saves `kv_start`, and the backward computes `q_end[b, k]`, one past the last query that attends key `k`, with `torch.searchsorted(kv_start, keys, right=True)`. That's exact because `kv_start` never decreases, and it takes 0.02 ms at 128k tokens.
- `kv_start` has to be an int32 `(batch, seqlen_q)` contiguous tensor, used on SM100/SM110 with `causal=True` (or `window_size=(left, 0)`). Varlen, paged KV, `qv`, `gather_kv_indices`, `mask_mod`, block sparsity and head dim 256 are rejected with an assert, and `num_splits` is forced to 1.
- Calls without `kv_start` are unchanged. The kernels get `None` in the new argument slot, and the compile key gains one boolean.

It works with GQA and `pack_gqa`, `window_size_left`, `softcap`, `score_mod`, `learnable_sink`, `deterministic=True`, `seqlen_q != seqlen_k` (bottom-right aligned, as with causal), and the 2-CTA backward at head dim 128 and up.

A query with `kv_start[i] = i + 1` sees no keys. Its output is 0, its LSE is -inf, and it gets no gradient.

`kv_start` must not decrease along the sequence. I didn't add a runtime check because it would need a device sync. If it does decrease, the results are wrong.

## Tests

On a B200 with torch 2.14.1+cu130 and nvidia-cutlass-dsl 4.8.0:

```shell
% pytest -W ignore -q tests/cute/test_flash_attn.py tests/cute/test_score_mod.py -k kv_start
288 passed, 418212 deselected in 655.80s (0:10:55)
```

- `test_flash_attn_kv_start` has 240 cases: head dims (64, 64), (128, 128) and (192, 128); 8/8 and 16/2 heads; seqlen (113, 113), (1000, 1000), (2048, 2048) and (1000, 1536); deterministic on and off; and five kinds of `kv_start`. Those are documents, documents with padding at the end, documents with a 64-token window folded in, documents plus `window_size=(63, 0)`, and a random non-decreasing `kv_start`. The reference is `attention_ref` with the equivalent dense mask, using the same tolerance rule as the rest of the file. It also checks that padding tokens get exactly zero output and gradients, and that deterministic runs agree bitwise. It works with the fake-tensor compile pass.
- `test_flash_attn_kv_start_softcap_sink` (32 cases) covers `softcap` and `learnable_sink`, including dSink.
- `test_cute_score_mod_with_kv_start` (16 cases) is the `flex_attention` comparison from section 2.

The only code existing calls go through is the left-mask boundary in `BlockInfo` and the extra `None` argument, so I ran the causal and local cases of the main test plus the `mask_mod` tests:

```shell
% tools/two_pass_tests.sh -g 0,1,2 -k "test_flash_attn_output, causal and local, d 64/128/192, softcap 0, no sink"
== pass 1: compile (FakeTensorMode, -n 48)
1872 passed in 174.85s
== pass 2: execute (GPUs 0,1,2, -n 3, compiles fail the test)
1872 passed in 51.18s
% pytest -n 3 tests/cute/test_mask_mod.py
835 passed, 748 skipped in 525.18s
```

## How I measured

One B200, bf16, torch 2.14.1+cu130, nvidia-cutlass-dsl 4.8.0. Each time is the median of `triton.testing.do_bench` with L2 flushed between runs. I ran the methods round-robin for 5 rounds (3 for the sequence-length sweep) and took the median round, so clock drift hits all of them the same way. Before timing, I checked each method's output against `kv_start`. Document lengths come from an exponential distribution with the given mean. Calls longer than 200 ms (single document at 1M and 2M) use the median of 3 runs timed with CUDA events.

- BlockMask: a document-causal `mask_mod` (two doc-id reads, like `cute_document_mask` in the tests, plus `n_idx <= m_idx`) with a `BlockMask` from `create_block_mask(..., BLOCK_SIZE=(256, 128), _compile=True)`, set up the same way `test_mask_mod.py` does on SM100.
- varlen: `flash_attn_varlen_func`, one sequence per document.
- kv_start: this PR.

The benchmark script is in this gist: https://gist.github.com/pashu-cohere/17e58a5f1be905ee43113a6431ffb55a. The sequence-length sweep and the `score_mod` table come from two small wrappers around it, which I can add too. I'm also happy to move it under `benchmarks/`.

## Limitations

- SM100/SM110 only. SM90 could get the same change in its mask and `BlockInfo`.
- Batched layout only. With varlen, documents can already be expressed as sequences.
- It only covers "causal from a per-query start". Bidirectional attention inside a document (prefix-LM) would need a per-row right edge as well, which would be the same change mirrored.
- It can't be combined with `mask_mod` (see section 2).
- I left the 2-CTA backward heuristic alone. For `kv_start`, 2-CTA is 3-13% faster in most cases, but with very short documents (mean length 256), 1-CTA wins by 4-5%.
- With one document at head dim 64, the `kv_start` backward is 2-4% slower than `causal=True`. Most of that comes from the local path it reuses (8 x 8k: causal 3.91 ms, `window_size=(S, 0)` 3.98 ms, `kv_start` 4.02 ms).

### Sliding window 4096 on top of documents

`mask_mod` is the BlockMask path. `mask_mod_kv256` is the same with 256-wide KV blocks. `mm_vec` is the BlockMask path with the vectorized `mask_mod` (forward only). `causal` is plain causal attention over the whole packed row; it ignores the documents, so it isn't the same result and is only there for scale. TFLOP/s counts attended (query, key) pairs only. Mask build is the time to make the mask from document ids.

items.title: fix(hd256/sm100): forward reads actual input strides, drop .contiguous() patch
items.body:
## Summary

  The dedicated SM100 hd256 2CTA forward kernel (`BlackwellFusedMultiHeadAttentionForward`) hardcoded contiguous strides for its q/k/v/o CUTE layouts, silently scrambling memory accesses for any caller passing a non-contiguous tensor — most notably the `(B, H, S, D).transpose(1, 2)` pattern used by HuggingFace attention layers. PR #2666 worked around this by forcing `q.contiguous() / k.contiguous() / v.contiguous()` in the dispatcher.

  This PR fixes the kernel itself so it reads the *actual* input strides, then removes the `.contiguous()` workaround. It also lifts the `_as_bshkrd_tensor` / `_as_shhb_tensor` helpers (already used by the hd256 backward) into a shared module.

 ## Changes

  - **`flash_attn/cute/utils.py`**  : module-level `as_bshkrd_tensor` and `as_shhb_tensor`, the rank-3/4/5 → canonical-view normalizers that preserve real input strides. Lifted verbatim from the backward.
  - **`flash_attn/cute/sm100_hd256_2cta_fmha_forward.py`**:  replaced the hardcoded layout strides with `as_bshkrd_tensor` normalization for q/k/v/o, then plugged the canonical strides into the existing `((h_r, h_k), b)` nested layout. The paged K/V path now uses the `cute.select(layout, mode=[1, 3, 2, 0])` / `cute.select(layout, mode=[3, 1, 2, 0])` idiom — the same one already used in `flash_fwd_sm100.py` for transpose-views  and reads the page table's real strides.
  - **`flash_attn/cute/sm100_hd256_2cta_fmha_backward.py`**:  deleted the local `_as_bshkrd_tensor` and `_as_shhb_tensor` defs; imports them from the shared utils module. No behavior change.
  - **`flash_attn/cute/interface.py`** — removed the `.contiguous()` workaround from PR #2666 (forward dispatch), the parallel `q/k/v/out/dout.contiguous()` block in the backward dispatch, and the now-unnecessary `page_table.stride(0) == page_table.shape[1]` contiguity assertion.

  ## Verification

  Tested on a B200 (sm100):

  - Dense MHA / GQA, causal and non-causal, head_dim=256, transpose-view q/k/v through `flash_attn_func`: output **bit-identical** to the contiguous reference (`max|view − contig| = 0`).
  - Varlen forward with non-contiguous q/k/v through `flash_attn_varlen_func`: output **bit-identical** to the contiguous reference.

  ## Note:

  This PR also removes the `.contiguous()` block from the **backward** dispatcher (the parallel block in `interface.py`); that block was already dead on compile-cache hits and the backward kernel handles real strides via `as_bshkrd_tensor` itself, so it's safe to drop.

items.title: [hd256] Add TMA paged KV support to SM100 2CTA forward kernel
items.body:
## Change

Add paged KV support to the SM100 hd256 2CTA forward kernel.

The paged path reuses the dense TMA load path. Logical KV blocks are remapped to physical page indices through the page table at load time, so each page maps to exactly one TMA tile.

**Constraint:** `page_size` must equal `tile_n = 128`.

### `flash_attn/cute/sm100_hd256_2cta_fmha_forward.py`

- Add conditional K/V tensor layouts in `__call__`:
  - Dense: `(s_k, d, ((h_r, h_k), b))`
  - Paged K: `(page_size, d, h_k, num_pages)`
  - Paged V uses the corresponding transposed layout.
- Add conditional K/V TMA setup in the load warp:
  - Dense path uses `domain_offset` + batch indexing.
  - Paged path slices by `head_kv` and keeps `num_pages` as the outer mode for per-load `page_idx` lookup.
- Add conditional per-load `page_idx` handling:
  - K uses mode-2 subtile + mode-3 page.
  - V uses mode-1 page.
- Plumb `mPageTable` and `max_seqlen_k` through the kernel signature.
- Use `max_seqlen_k` for `seqlen_k` in all four warp sections on the paged path.
- Store `qhead_per_kvhead` on `self` and derive `head_kv_coord` via integer division, matching `flash_fwd_sm100` for contiguous GQA grouping.
- Relax `mPageTable` / `paged_kv_non_tma` assertions.

### `flash_attn/cute/paged_kv.py`

- Extract `_flatten_smem_sm100` and `_copy_row_async` helpers from `load_KV`.
- Pure refactor with no behavior change for existing callers.

### `tests/cute/test_flash_attn.py`

- Add `test_flash_attn_paged_hd256_sm100_tma`
  - Bit-exact vs dense varlen reference.
  - Includes determinism check.
  - Parameterized over `seqlen_q`.
- Add `test_flash_attn_paged_hd256_sm100_tma_gqa`
  - Same checks for GQA with `nheads_kv in {2, 4, 8}`.
  - Exercises `qhead_per_kvhead > 1`, which would expose modulo-aliasing bugs.

---

## Validation (this PR vs `origin/main` @ `b21e204`)

### Correctness Smoke Test

Ran `pytest tests/cute/test_flash_attn.py` on B200 with the 6 new paged tests plus the existing dense d=256 subset:

```bash
-k "paged_hd256_sm100_tma or (test_flash_attn_output and 256-False-0-0.0-False-False)"
```

Result: **84 passed, 78 skipped, 0 failed** in 2 minutes.

The **78 skipped** cases come from the existing dense d=256 subset (same pass/skip count as `origin/main`), and **6 passing tests** are from the new `paged_hd256_sm100_tma[_gqa]` coverage.

### Forward Performance Delta vs `origin/main`

TFLOPS mean over 3 runs each.  
Platform: B200, bf16, hdim=256, locked clocks @ 1755 MHz.

| Seqlen | Causal | MHA 32:32 | GQA 32:2 |
|------:|:------:|----------:|---------:|
| 4k    | F | +0.2% | +0.3% |
| 8k    | F | 0.0% | -0.1% |
| 16k   | F | -0.2% | 0.0% |
| 32k   | F | -1.0% | **+2.3%** |
| 64k   | F | **+2.1%** | +0.8% |
| 128k  | F | -0.8% | -1.7% |
| 4k    | T | +0.2% | +0.2% |
| 8k    | T | +0.1% | +0.1% |
| 16k   | T | +0.3% | +0.1% |
| 32k   | T | **+3.0%** | -1.2% |
| 64k   | T | -0.3% | -0.1% |
| 128k  | T | +0.1% | -0.7% |

### Summary

- **22 of 24 cells are within ±2%.**
- The two `>2%` outliers are both positive and fall within the batch-quantization noise zone observed during the baseline sweep.
- Aggregated means:
  - **MHA: +0.31%**
  - **GQA: +0.00%**
- `benchmark_attn.py` uses contiguous KV, so the paged path is not exercised there.
- Dense-path parity is the regression-critical requirement and is preserved.

PR authored by @Johnsonms @Orion34-lanbo and @yunzhongOvO

items.title: [CuTe, SM100] hd256 2-CTA: support seqused_q/seqused_k and the decoder paged-KV shape
items.body:
## Problem

The dedicated SM100/SM110 head-dim 256 2-CTA forward kernel asserts off per-batch actual
sequence lengths:

```
AssertionError: SM100 forward with head_dim=256 does not support seqused_q/seqused_k
```

`seqused_k` is exactly what continuous-batching inference servers supply for decoder
attention over a paged KV cache. As a direct consequence, vLLM disabled FA4 head-dim 256
on Blackwell entirely on 2026-08-16 (vllm-project/vllm#52050, "[Bugfix] Temporarily
disable FA4 head-dim 256"), stating:

> PR #42669 enabled FA4 head-dim 256 on Blackwell, but the specialized SM100 2-CTA kernel
> still rejects `seqused_q/k`, which vLLM decoder attention supplies. Temporarily resolve
> FA2 for head-dim 256 on Blackwell until upstream adds the required support. FA4 remains
> enabled for head-dim 128 and the supported MLA 192/128 case.

This PR implements that support in the forward kernel, and adapts the adjacent paged-KV
calling contract that blocks the same path, so head-dim 256 models can run FA4 on
Blackwell under continuous batching again.

## What changed

**`flash_attn/cute/sm100_hd256_2cta_fmha_forward.py`**

The dedicated kernel does not use `SeqlenInfoQK`; it threads per-work-tile
`seqlen_q`/`seqlen_k` scalars inline into `FusedMask.get_trip_start_count_via_block_info`
and the epilogue/LSE predication. This change keeps that inline convention and overrides
the two scalars with the per-batch `seqused` values at the four work-tile setup sites
(load, MMA, softmax, correction/epilogue), with the same precedence
`SeqlenInfoQK.create` implements in the general SM100 kernel:

- `seqused_q`/`seqused_k` win for the *lengths*;
- `cu_seqlens_q`/`cu_seqlens_k` continue to provide the packing *offsets*.

Two properties the placement guarantees:

- **Warp lockstep.** When `seqused_q` shrinks a batch below a q tile, the work-skip
  predicate (`continue_cond`) is recomputed with the identical expression in every warp
  section, so the load, MMA, softmax and correction pipelines agree on which work tiles
  are skipped (same discipline as the varlen `cu_seqlens_q` path today).
- **No new out-of-bounds exposure.** `seqused_* <= ` allocated lengths only ever *shrink*
  trip counts relative to the existing static/varlen values; tail positions inside the
  last KV tile are masked to exact-zero probability exactly as the varlen path already
  does. Zero-length batches ride the existing zero-trip clamp.

The `mSeqUsedQ`/`mSeqUsedK` parameters already existed in `__call__` for interface parity
(marked TODO); they are now forwarded into the device kernel. The interface compile key
already contained `seqused_q is None` / `seqused_k is None`, so the no-seqused
specialization is byte-identical to before — **zero impact when seqused is not passed**
(all new device code is behind `cutlass.const_expr`).

**`flash_attn/cute/interface.py`**

- Remove the `seqused_q is None and seqused_k is None` assert from the
  `use_dedicated_hd256_kernel` forward branch. The surrounding plumbing (tensor
  normalization, compile args, call args, compile key) already passed seqused through;
  only the assert blocked it.
- Add one loud guard: `cu_seqlens_k` without `cu_seqlens_q` is rejected for this kernel.
  The dedicated kernel derives its K/V load offsets from the varlen-Q block, so
  varlen-packed K without varlen Q would read every batch from offset 0 (silently wrong).
  This mode was previously unreachable only because the seqused assert happened to block
  the test path into it; with seqused enabled it must be rejected explicitly. (No known
  caller uses this combination; vLLM uses `cu_seqlens_q` + `page_table` + `seqused_k`.)

**`flash_attn/cute/interface.py` — paged-KV extent/page-table contract**

Removing the `seqused` assert alone does *not* re-open the decoder path, because the same
branch also asserts, for paged KV:

```python
assert max_seqlen_k % page_size == 0
assert page_table.shape[1] == max_seqlen_k // page_size
```

(pre-existing code, not introduced here — its own message tells the caller to
`pass page_table[:, :N]`). A continuous-batching decoder cannot satisfy either one:
`max_seqlen_k` is the *current batch maximum* sequence length, which is arbitrary and
rarely a multiple of the page size, and `page_table` has a fixed width sized for the
largest supported context, independent of the current batch. In vLLM's decoder call
these come straight from the batch metadata (`seqused_k = seq_lens`,
`max_seqlen_k = max_seq_len` — the batch max — and `block_table`, the full-width table).
So a decode step with, say, `max_seqlen_k = 257` and a 256-column table trips both
asserts even with `seqused_k` support in place.

This PR therefore normalizes the two values in the interface instead of requiring the
caller to pre-slice: round the KV extent up to the enclosing page and narrow the table to
match.

```python
required_pages = (max_seqlen_k + page_size - 1) // page_size
assert page_table.shape[1] >= required_pages      # genuinely-too-small table: still loud
page_table = page_table[:, :required_pages]
max_seqlen_k = required_pages * page_size
```

Three properties worth checking in review:

- **Placement.** It runs *before* `_get_fwd_config`, before the compile key, and before
  the page-table tensor conversion, so tile selection, kernel specialization and the
  device-side tensor all see the same normalized values. (`max_seqlen_k` reaches the
  compile key indirectly, through the tile sizes `_get_fwd_config` picks.)
- **Rounding is bounded by `seqused_k`, and that is enforced.** Widening the extent is
  only faithful to the caller if each sequence is still bounded at its true length.
  `seqused_k` is that bound — positions in `[seqused_k, rounded)` mask to exact-zero
  probability, exactly like the existing intra-tile tail. If `max_seqlen_k` needs
  rounding and no `seqused_k` is given, the interface now refuses loudly rather than
  silently letting every sequence attend the remainder of its last page. The kernel side
  is consistent by construction: it derives its paged extent as
  `mPageTable.shape[1] * page_size`, which is exactly the normalized `max_seqlen_k`.
- **No behavior change for callers that already met the contract.** When `max_seqlen_k`
  is page-aligned and the table is exactly `max_seqlen_k // page_size` wide,
  `required_pages` equals the existing width, the slice is a no-op and the extent is
  unchanged — the existing paged hd256 tests are bit-identical.

This is a deliberate contract change: it moves the slicing from the caller into the
interface. The argument for it is that the contract as written cannot be met by the
consumer this kernel exists to serve, and the normalization is exactly the slice the
assert message already asks for. If you would rather keep the contract caller-side, the
alternative is a documented helper plus a change on the vLLM side; happy to go that way
instead.

The head-dim 256 **backward** still rejects `seqused_q/seqused_k` (unchanged); forward
inference is what unblocks the serving use case.

## Tests

**`tests/cute/test_flash_attn.py`**

- `test_flash_attn_varlen_output`: drop the d=256 skip of the seqused modes
  (`unpad_q/unpad_kv = False`). The existing matrix now exercises, for hd256:
  per-batch random lengths, `seqused_q`-only, `seqused_k`-only, both, zero-length
  batches, seqused == full length (`varlen_mode="full"`), across the existing
  seqlen/causal/GQA/dtype grid — all against the PyTorch reference. The backward leg
  stays restricted to the fully-unpadded mode (hd256 backward does not support seqused
  yet); a narrow skip remains for the unsupported varlen-K-without-varlen-Q combination,
  matching the new interface guard.
- New `test_flash_attn_paged_hd256_sm100_tma_seqused_k` (mirrors the existing
  `test_flash_attn_paged_hd256_sm100_tma*` family): paged KV with a `page_table` wider
  than the batch needs and per-batch `seqused_k` of {page-aligned, one past a page
  boundary, mid-page}, for q=1 (decode) and q>1, parametrized over both callers —
  `max_seqlen_k` as the **batch maximum** (257: neither page-aligned nor equal to
  `page_table.shape[1] * page_size`, the shape the decoder actually passes, and the case
  that fails without the normalization above) and `max_seqlen_k` page-aligned at the
  allocated capacity (what a caller that pre-slices passes). Both are checked against a
  dense varlen reference over the true per-batch lengths. Everything past each
  sequence's `seqused_k` — the tail inside its last page and every page after it — is
  poisoned with large finite values, and the test asserts the output is finite and stays
  within the reference's magnitude range, so a leak past `seqused_k` (e.g. if the rounded
  extent were not masked) fails loudly instead of drifting. Finite poison rather than
  NaN is deliberate: masked positions still contribute `0 * value` to the PV
  accumulation, so `0 * NaN` would poison a correct kernel too.
  `seqused_k == allocated length` is asserted **bitwise identical** to not passing
  `seqused_k`.
- New `test_flash_attn_paged_hd256_sm100_tma_contract_guards`: asserts both normalization
  guards fire — a `page_table` too narrow for the requested extent, and an extent that
  needs rounding with no `seqused_k` to bound the sequences.

## Testing done / not done

- Static validation of this branch: `py_compile`, AST-level checks of the four device
  sites, launch/signature ordering against the interface compile/call argument order.
- **Run on B300 (SM103) hardware against this exact source**, covering the decoder shapes
  this PR is about:

  | case | result |
  |---|---|
  | `max_seqlen_k=257` (batch max, not page-aligned) against a full four-column page table — the shape the old assert rejected | pass, max err vs fp32 ref `1.95e-3` |
  | page-aligned capacity path | pass, and bit-identical to the current-max output |
  | `q=120` paged causal | pass, max err `7.81e-3` |
  | CUDA Graph captured at KV length 64, replayed after `seqused_k` grew to 129 | pass, max err `1.95e-3` |

  Errors are at the bf16 floor for these shapes.
- A functionally equivalent patch (same per-batch overrides at the same four work-tile
  sites) has additionally been exercised at length on SM103 under vLLM with paged KV
  (page size 128), q=1 decode and prefill — but against vLLM's vendored
  `vllm-flash-attn` copy, which has diverged from this repo.
- **Not covered:** the zero-length paged-KV edge was not executed on hardware. It is not
  part of the decoder contract this PR targets (vLLM does not issue zero-length KV in this
  path), and the kernel's existing zero-trip clamp and zero/NaN `row_sum` guards are what
  make it well-defined — but it is a hardening case rather than a validated one. Narrowing
  the test skip also means the varlen suite now runs `seqused_k` together with zero-length
  sequences for the first time; that is the case I would watch first in CI.

## Relationship to #2749

Semantically orthogonal: #2749 enables causal-left local attention for this same kernel
by removing the adjacent `is_local`/`window_size` asserts; this PR does not touch those
asserts, and neither feature depends on the other. A trial merge of the two branches
shows `sm100_hd256_2cta_fmha_forward.py` merges clean; `interface.py` and the test
skip block conflict textually (both PRs edit adjacent lines), which is a few-line
resolution for whichever lands second. The combination (per-batch `seqused_k` +
causal-left sliding window) has been exercised together on SM103, so the two features are
known to compose.

items.title: [FA4][hd256] Backward TMA bulk-store epilogue + LSE/dpsum coalesce
items.body:
## Summary

Two commits targeting the `sm100_hd256_2cta_fmha_backward` kernels on Blackwell (B200):

**Commit 1 — `1748c9a`: Coalesce LSE/dpsum per-K-iter loads in dkdv**

- Replaces scattered per-thread indexing (`thread_idx * N + i`) with warp-coalesced indexing (`thread_idx + i * threads_per_warp`) for LSE and dpsum GMEM→SMEM loads in the dkdv accumulation loop. Applied at three sites (init, main loop, CLC path). Eliminates the strided-load hotspot lines `:1922` and `:1953` from the ncu profile.

**Commit 2 — `ed71d51`: TMA bulk-store epilogue for dK/dV and dQ**

- **dkdv kernel**: Replaces per-thread scattered GMEM stores in the dK/dV epilogue (the top 1 ncu bottleneck — 2.8B excess global sectors, 71–96% of all uncoalesced traffic) with a cooperative TMA bulk-store path. Both warp-groups write into a CTA-shared `(64, 256)` SMEM tile (aliased onto the dead `sP+sdST` buffers), then WG 0's leader fires 4 × `(64, 64)` `cp.async.bulk.tensor` stores.
- **dq kernel**: Adds a single-stage rotating TMA bulk-store epilogue for dQ (aliased onto the consumed `sdO` SMEM), eliminating the per-thread store hotspot at `dqkernel.py:2143` (70 MB excess sectors, 95.5% of dq residual).
- Per-thread `self.store` is retained as a fallback for the varlen path in both kernels.

**Commit 3 — 62d1304: Fix TMA epilogue OOB writes on residual K/Q tiles**
                                                                                                           
- The TMA bulk-store paths introduced in commit 2 write a full (64, 64) or (128, 64) tile unconditionally, causing out-of-bounds GMEM writes when the sequence dimension is not evenly divisible by the tile size.  
                                                            
- dkdv kernel: Gates the TMA dV/dK paths on a full-tile predicate ((blk_coord_k + 1) * tile_shape_K <=  seqlen_k). Residual tiles — where the K block extends past seqlen_k — fall back to the per-thread self.store() path, which already carries per-element elem_less bounds checks. The varlen path already bypassed TMA and continues to use self.store() unconditionally.

- dq kernel: Threads tile_q_start (= curr_block_coord[0] * cta_tiler[0]) through tma_args into dQ_epilogue. Each epilogue iteration checks tile_q_start + (iter + 1) * epi_tile[0] <= seqlen_q; partial Q tiles fall back to the autovec_copy path with elem_less masking. Applied uniformly across the non-varlen path; the varlen path was already on the fallback. 

### Why CTA-shared (not per-WG) for dkdv

At hd=256 the epilogue t2r atom (`tcgen05.copy.Ld32x32bOp(Repetition(32))`) gives each WG interleaved N-coverage: `{0..31, 64..95, 128..159, 192..223}` for WG 0, complementary for WG 1. TMA requires contiguous SMEM → contiguous GMEM. That invariant cannot be satisfied per-WG when data is interleaved across the full 256-column range. The CTA-shared design has both WGs cooperatively populate one `(64, 256)` virtual tile, then WG 0 issues all 4 TMA boxes.

## Files changed

- `flash_attn/cute/sm100_hd256_2cta_fmha_backward_dkdvkernel.py`
- `flash_attn/cute/sm100_hd256_2cta_fmha_backward_dqkernel.py`

## ncu highlights (B200, vs original baseline `4819cf2`)

| Kernel | Excess global sectors | SM throughput | Cycles/inst |
|---|---|---|---|
| A_dkdv (non-causal) | 2 818 M → **0** (-100%) | 72.1% → **85.7%** | 16.2 → **13.45** (-17%) |
| B_dkdv (causal) | 2 422 M → **0** (-100%) | 47.7% → **61.4%** | 10.9 → ~10 |
| A_dq | 70 M → **~0** | 82.3% → 82.4% | 17.5 → 17.5 |
| B_dq | 70 M → **~0** | 87.2% → 87.1% | 16.2 → 16.2 |

dkdv is now tensor-pipe-bound as intended. L1 hit-rate collapse on dkdv (88% → 0%) is expected: TMA bulk stores bypass L1 entirely.

## Benchmark (B200 @ 1755 MHz, rep=50)

Baseline: `1748c9a` (LSE-coalesce commit, pre-TMA-epilogue).
After: `ed71d51` (this branch tip).

### MHA (nheads=32, nheads_kv=32)

| seqlen | Baseline TFLOPS | After TFLOPS | Δ% |
|-------:|----------------:|-------------:|---:|
| **Non-causal** | | | |

### GQA (nheads=32, nheads_kv=2)
